rules.K1: example: a fenced code block that is an example (K12 predicate false): it lies in an examples or non-normative section or passage, its info string carries a key=value witness tag, or a preceding statement of its clause is an example (K6) or names an example / witness / sample / illustration
rules.K2: non-normative: the section or an enclosing section is front matter, a change log (title 'Changes from ...') or titled *(non-normative)* / *(deferred)*
rules.K3: non-normative: the sentence starts with *(non-normative...)* or *(deferred...)* (the marker scopes its own sentence only); uncertain if it contains an RFC 2119 keyword
rules.K4: requirement: contains an upper-case RFC 2119 keyword (MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL, REQUIRED, ...)
rules.K5: definition: introduces a defined term (bold) or a rule label of its clause as the subject being defined ('X is/are/means/denotes ...', 'X = ...', 'X: <noun phrase>', 'X (...):', '... is the X'), or carries a term whose sentence is otherwise a verbless fragment ('**Tier.** CC, R, Q.'), or is a verbless id-table row naming what its label stands for
rules.K6: example: starts with e.g. / For example / Example, contains e.g., or lies in an examples section
rules.K7: requirement: lower-case normative word (must, must not, cannot, shall, may only, may not, never)
rules.K8: requirement: a declarative verb from the fixed list (is, are, returns, rejects, traps, ...)
rules.K9: requirement: a table row (normative table: instruction, default, error-code rows state their content in columns, not sentences)
rules.K10: uncertain: none of the above (verbless fragment, list-item fragment)
rules.K11: sub-statement classified K10 inherits the kind of its enumerating sentence
rules.K12: requirement, or definition when the introducing statement is one: a fenced code block that is not an example (K1 predicate false): a normative table, grammar, schema or listing
rules.K13: requirement: carries a term or rule label of its clause (recorded in defines) that it does not introduce (run-in caption '**X.** <rule>', inline bold term, label row), and states a rule (K7/K8 test), or a label caption outside a table heads a verbless remainder ('**T5.** As §6.3.')
rules.K14: definition: verbless equation 'X = ...', 'X := ...', '... ≡ ...' (X a name or code span)
rules.K15: requirement: verbless colon-labelled fragment 'Label: content' or a bare colon introduction 'Frames:' (field and list stems of a normative text)
rules.K16: kind of the previous statement (requirement or definition): a verbless fragment that follows a statement of its clause, or opens a list item continuing the previous clause of its section

statements.text: **Status:** draft 0.2.10 of `bennett-dialect-spec` (`Bennett-NorthStar.md` §3, §6.1), written from the ratified outline `spec/outline-0.2.md` (maintainer rulings of 2026-10-29 at its end), revised after council rounds 1–3.
It replaces draft 0.1, which the narrowing audit (`docs/audit/2026-10-29-dialect-0.1-narrowing-audit.md`) found to narrow north-star scope in 40 distinct places.
Nothing is implemented.
It targets the Bennett virtual ISA **draft 0.8** (`bennett-isa-spec/spec/Bennett-ISA-Spec.md`, council accepted 2026-10-28), cited "ISA §n", and is graded against ISA 0.8.
MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are normative; *(non-normative)* explains.
Mechanics this draft does not settle carry a **default** in §24; capabilities that ISA 0.8 cannot express in some case are **blockers** in §25, each with the exact ISA change.

**Versioning.** Dialect 0.2.10: markers 0.2, handles 0.2.8, regions 0.2.8, oracle-abi 0.2.4, tdl 0.2.4, effects 0.2.4, norm 0.2.8, map 0.2.9, asm 0.2, platform 0.2.1, driver 0.2.1, corpus 0.2; targets ISA 0.8.
The **full version string** (`0.2.10`) is the compatibility unit (§23): drafts are not compatible with each other.

**Standing rule (CLAUDE.md rule 10; council rubric S0).** This document narrows no capability that the north star promises (its thesis, §3–§5 and every rung of the §8 demo ladder; Grover over unmodified SQLite is the core).
It rejects at compile time only what the north star itself requires to be rejected or what a maintainer decision settles; every such rejection is a row of §22.1 citing the clause or decision.
A deferral (§24) postpones mechanics only and states the capability it keeps.

Where ISA 0.8 cannot express a promised capability in some case, the dialect still specifies the whole mechanism, states the ISA 0.8 realisation that exists for the other cases, and names a blocker (§25) whose verdict is `blocked:`, never `reject:`.

**Sources.** North star §0, §3, §4, §5, §8; the legality spike and its findings (`docs/spikes/2026-10-28-legality-findings.md`, decisions 1–4); the narrowing audit (row ids D1–D25, B-01–B-55, O-01–O-08, G-12–G-16, ISA-1–ISA-11 are cited unchanged); the rung-4 spike (`docs/spikes/sqlite/REPORT.md`, cited "SQLite §n"); the outline (cited "outline", decisions B1–B17, questions E1–E14).

The dialect is the contract between **front ends** that emit LLVM IR containing calls to `__bennett_*` marker functions and the **plugin** that, at the final link of a whole program, recognises those calls, analyses and normalises the code they reach, and maps it onto the ISA (ISA §1.1).
It fixes:
the marker ABI, operand encodings and C header (§3);
the processing order, execution tiers, polyvariant variants and function addresses (§4);
the device analysis: points-to, value sets and every question answered from them (§5);
the handle convention, provenance, comparison and collections of handles (§6);
regions: kinds, candidate sets, dispatch, identity, well-formedness (§7);
the oracle interface: the descriptor, parameter and device bindings, entry state, wide outputs and in-place updates (§8);
budgets (§9);
taint-driven lifting of classical code under control (§10);
effects and device models per tier (§11);
the materialised normalisation and the residual-poison validator (§12), floating point (§13), calls and control transfer (§14), inline asm and target intrinsics (§15);
the lifting map from materialised LLVM to ISA objects (§16);
the device classical memory model, CC and R lowering rules and fault outcomes (§17);
a reference semantics from marker programs to the ISA formal model (§18);
the driver's modes and plugin-invocation interface (§19);
the platform profile `riscv64-bennett-virt` (§20);
the legality corpus and conformance suites (§21); diagnostics (§22); versioning (§23); deferred mechanics (§24); blockers and ISA items (§25).
It does not fix the plugin's optimisation pipeline after normalisation, the plugin's device objects beyond the constraints of §18.7, or any format the ISA owns.
Producer | front ends (clang, rustc, Bennett.jl, importers) | emit modules that satisfy §3 and the outlining conventions of §7.6; never emit a reserved name of §3.1 other than a marker

Plugin | `bennett-plugin` and competitors | the processing order of §4.1; give every module the verdict the rules give it, with the diagnostics of §22; produce ISA objects whose execution equals the reference semantics (§18.7); suites DA–DX (§21.3)

Driver | `bennett-driver` | §19; links `bennett-runtimes` and `bennett-arith` bitcode of the link's LLVM major (§19.1); builds the comparison link and the native comparison binary (§17.7); emits blocker reports (§25)
Validator | the plugin's validator and `bennett-conformance` | the residual-poison validator (§12.4) and the reference recogniser (§3, §5, §6, §7), implemented independently; suites DA–DN

Runtime | `bennett-runtimes` and `bennett-arith` | define every entry point that §11, §13, §14, §17 and §20 name (prefixes `__bennett_rt_`, `__bennett_dev_`, `__bennett_sf_`, §3.1) with the semantics stated there, as ordinary bitcode compiled by the same pipeline; suites DR and DF
Platform | a platform profile of §20 | a board model plus shims satisfying §20; suite DP
`scripts/dialect_check.py` in this repository is the seed of the pre-flight checker (§1.5).
It never bounds this document: an example it cannot yet execute fails the check (rule P-2, §1.5).
The ISA is settled; this document never redefines it.

Every ISA notion used here (tiers, wires, `qreg` handles, oracles, actions, permutation actions, lprocs, F_B, budgets, tokens, fault codes, the reference interpreter, interface and closure hashes, layouts, the launch ABI) has exactly the meaning ISA §2–§17 give it.

Where the dialect needs a construct ISA 0.8 lacks, this document states (a) the full dialect mechanism, (b) its realisation on ISA 0.8 where one exists, which may be a longer construction (an **efficiency item**, §25.3), and (c) otherwise a **blocker** (§25.1) naming the exact ISA change.
(a) the full dialect mechanism
(b) its realisation on ISA 0.8 where one exists, which may be a longer construction (an **efficiency item**, §25.3)
(c) otherwise a **blocker** (§25.1) naming the exact ISA change.
The dialect never shrinks to fit the ISA and never extends the ISA unilaterally.
Only these remain.
Every row of 0.1 §1.4 that narrowed scope (1.4-d, 1.4-e, 1.4-f) is deleted; its replacement is §10, §9 and §8.7 respectively.

§3.1 handle row: a handle through an `inttoptr`/`ptrtoint` round trip is rejected | Provenance flows through bitwise copies (§6.2) | Spike F1; maintainer decision 2; north-star amendment A2 (drafted with A1, bd `-25h`)

§3.1: regions entered as `__bennett_ctrl(q, @f, …)` with a constant `@f` | Region operands are classical data dispatched over a candidate set bounded by the program (§7.2) | Spike F3; maintainer decision 3
Region named by symbol | Region identity is by content (§7.3) | Spike F2; maintainer decision 1
§3.1 handle row is silent on comparison | `icmp eq/ne` of handles is identity (§6.3) | Maintainer decision 4 (2026-10-29; legality findings §3); a superset

§3.1, §4.2: a `qstore` into a register not known to be clean is a compile-time error | `qstore` is the ISA's XOR store; the compile-time rule is an optional warning `BD-W-QSTORE-UNCLEAN` (§6.7) | A register-granularity rule forbids the uncomputing second store; a superset of the north star (audit 1.4-g, D7)

§3.2: normalisation of "the outlined region" | Normalisation applies to every device variant (§12.1) | Device CC code is lowered to ISA CC, whose semantics differs from LLVM's poison semantics (ISA §4.1); a superset (audit 1.4-h)
LLVM IR is LLVM's textual form with opaque pointers, as accepted by LLVM 18, 20 and 23.
`P(a)` is the representation width of an integral pointer in address space a from DataLayout, falling back to the default pointer entry (64 with no entry).
`pw=P(0)` is the ISA address width, not the width of every LLVM pointer.
`I(a)` is its independently specified pointer-index width (default P(a)).
Numbers are decimal unless written `0x…`.
A(F) is the function address of §4.4.
**Process rules** (also in `spec/README.md`):

**P-1.** Every mechanism rule id (the steps S1–S9, rules N1–N35, V1–V16, TDL-1–TDL-12, the points-to rules PT1–PT12, the binding kinds of §8.2, the transforms of §14, the map rows of §16.4) has at least one checked `accept` example; every compile-time rejection of §22.1 has one `reject` example; every blocker of §25.1 has one `blocked` example.
Appendix B is the index, and the checker derives it from the text: a rule id with no example fails the check.
**P-2.** An example that the checker cannot yet execute **fails** the check with `checker-unimplemented: <capability>`.
It is never skipped, and this document never removes or weakens an example to make the checker pass.
The freeze gate is an all-green check.
**P-3.** Every executed result comes from an independent executor: LLVM tools, natively built binaries, or the Rust ISA reference interpreter `bennett-isa-ref`.
Python computes only *expected* artefacts (recogniser verdicts, normaliser output, map output, TDL events), and is never both producer and judge of one example.
Every fenced block whose info string starts with `llvm`, `isa`, `c`, `rust`, `julia`, `json` or `text` followed by a tag below is a **checked example**.
Its attributes are `key=value` pairs.

The last column names the checker capability (Appendix B) and, where the ISA reference interpreter is the executor, the `bennett-isa-ref` command (`check`, `hash`, `run-oracle`, `step-check` exist; `run-cc`, `reverse`, `run-action`, `run-program` are requested, bd `b-isa-spec-xam`).
`llvm markers-ir` | the marker list of §3.2; compared with the C view | `parse`, `header`
`c markers-c` | the prototypes of the C header; byte-equal to `spec/bennett_markers.h` between its BEGIN/END PROTOTYPES lines | `header`
`llvm example=ID verdict=V` | a module; it parses and verifies on LLVM 18, 20 and 23 and the reference recogniser gives verdict `V` (`accept`, `reject:<code>` or `blocked:<code>`, §1.6).

Optional attributes: `candidates=f,g` (the resolved candidate set of the first region operand, §7.2), `callees=f,g` (the candidate set of the first indirect call, §14.2), `shapes=N` (the number of compiled oracle shapes, §8.4), `mode=validate` (validator only, §12.4), `rmode=@f` (compiled in the whole-program R mode with entry f, §19.2) | `parse`, `recognise`

`llvm normalise-in=ID` / `llvm normalise-out=ID` | the normaliser (§12) applied to the first gives the second, lines compared after collapsing runs of blanks; both verify on the three majors (a source-only `majors=23` tag limits a form introduced in LLVM 23); the second passes the validator | `parse`, `normalise`

`text native=ID` | inputs and outputs of the native differential of a normalisation pair or a lifted example: both modules (or the C source and the module) built natively with the seeds of `spec/seeds/` (§21.4), run on the listed inputs, outputs equal to the listed values | `native`

`llvm lift=ID` | a materialised module; attribute `region=@f` names the region function and `desc=` the binding shape: the parameters' bindings in order (`IN(n,zext)`, `IN(n,sext)`, `ARG(W)`, `MEM_IN(A)`, `OUT(size)`), then `;dev=` device bindings (`ENTROPY(A)`, …) and `;tgt=` n(tgt) | `parse`, `map`

`text linkmap=ID` | the comparison-link facts the map of `lift=ID` reads (§19.5): `null_size`, `heap_base`, `heap_limit_max`, the globals with their bases, the A(F) of address-taken functions, and the budget table's largest `heap` and `stack` | `map`
`isa object=ID` | the reference object (§16.2) that the map produces from `lift=ID`, as complete ISA text; byte-equal to the map output; `bennett-isa-ref check` accepts it | `map`, `check`
`text hash=ID` | the interface hashes of the object's symbols (`bennett-isa-ref hash`) | `hash`

`text run=ID` | lines `input=… [mem=name:hex] [arg=…] budget=s,h,st,d -> code=C payload=P steps=N`; each line is the output of `bennett-isa-ref run-oracle <object> ref` with those options | `run-oracle`
`text step-check=ID` | a prefix-reversal claim; the output of `bennett-isa-ref step-check <object> ref --exhaustive` with the stated options | `step-check`
`llvm semantics=ID corpus=NAME` | a marker program; byte-equal to `corpus/legality/cases/NAME.ll`; run through the trace runtime and the reference semantics (§18) | `trace`, `run-action`
`text events=ID` / `text state=ID` | the event list (§18.2) of a marker program on an input, and the state vector before event `at` | `trace`, `run-action`
`text tdl=ID` | the TDL partition (§10, TDL-3) and generated event list of an action region invocation | `tdl`, `run-action`
`text cc-run=ID` | a CC or R run: results, fault records, tape, and the state after `bennett_reverse` | `run-cc`, `reverse`
`text blocker=ID` | the blocker report (§25.1) the plugin emits for a `blocked:` example | `recognise`
`json budget-table=ID` | a budget table (§9.2); parsed and resolved against the example it names | `driver`

`c example=ID`, `rust example=ID`, `julia example=ID` | a source file compiled by the toolchains of `corpus/legality/toolchains.toml` (`clang -O2 -flto` on 18, 20, 23, with `-I spec`; with `rmode=` against the `bennett-runtimes` musl sysroot, for which the checker's seeds stand in; `rustc --emit=llvm-bc`; Julia `code_llvm`) and then `lto<O3>`; the result is recognised with verdict `verdict=V` | `frontend`, `recognise`
A module example that calls a marker or a primitive without declaring it implicitly contains its declaration (§3.2, §3.1).

**Section references**: `§n` is a section of this document, `ISA §n` of the ISA specification, `NS §n` of `Bennett-NorthStar.md`; a reference that continues a list (`ISA §4.7, §5.3`) names the same document as the reference before it.
Fenced blocks without a tag are illustrations and are non-normative; an `llvm` or `isa` block without a tag is an error of this document.
A module's **verdict** is one of:
`accept`: the plugin produces its objects;
`reject:<code>`: a compile-time rejection of §22.1.
The plugin MUST fail the compilation (nonzero exit, no output object) and report at least the first diagnostic in the processing order of §4.1;
`blocked:<code>`: the module is accepted by the dialect, but at least one program point needs a capability that ISA 0.8 cannot express (§25.1).

The plugin MUST produce its objects with every such point lowered to a **blocker trap** (§25.1: a run-time fault on exactly the executions that reach the point), MUST emit the blocker report of §25.1 and MUST exit with the distinct status 3.
The code is the first blocker report in processing order.
The R-entry BLK-5 classification of §11.5 and §25.1 applies even when all supplied budgets allow a successful execution; §17.6 defines its mandatory typed fault point.
A module that would be rejected and blocked is rejected.
Warnings (`BD-W-*`, §22.4) never change a verdict.
**Marker**: one of the 23 functions of §3.2.
**Marker call**: a `call` or `invoke` whose callee is a marker (§3.5).
**Effect marker**: one of the five `__bennett_effect_*` markers.
**Primitive**: a reserved function with prefix `__bennett_nz_` that the map lowers to an ISA instruction directly (§3.1, §16.4): `__bennett_nz_fault`, `__bennett_nz_alloc`, `__bennett_nz_free`.
**Runtime entry point**: a function with prefix `__bennett_rt_`, `__bennett_dev_` or `__bennett_sf_` that `bennett-runtimes` or `bennett-arith` defines in bitcode (§3.1).
**Handle**: the `ptr` value a `__bennett_qalloc` or `__bennett_qborrow` call returns; it denotes a **register** of n qubits, the ISA's `qreg[n]` (ISA §3.3).
Qubit `i` of a handle is a **wire**.
**Register tag**: the opaque value (nonzero, below 2^pw) that represents a handle in device memory and in integers; at the host–device boundary a handle is an ISA launch register id (§6.1).
**Root**: an allocation of a register, identified by its allocation site and dynamic instance index (§6.5).
**Handle-derived**: a value whose provenance (§6.2) contains a root.
**Region function**: a function a region-entry marker receives.
**Region operand**: the marker operand that names it.
**Candidate set**: the functions a region operand can denote (§7.2).
**Action region**: a candidate of a `ctrl`, `adj` or `compute` operand; its interface is a quantum action (ISA §5.3).
**Oracle region**: a candidate of an `oracle` or `inplace` operand; its interface is a lifted oracle (ISA §5.2).
**Reversible region**: a candidate of a `reversible` operand, or the whole-program entry of §19.2; R-tier code (ISA §3.1).
**Tier** of a function variant: **H** (host, native), **CC** (device classical control, ISA §3.1), **R** (reversible, ISA §3.1), **L** (lifted: an lproc or oracle body, ISA §3.7).
A **variant** is a (function, tier, coherence signature) triple (§4.3); host code keeps the original function, every device tier gets a clone.
**Device program**: every variant of tier CC, R or L.
**Device entry**: a device variant called by an H function (a launch, ISA §10).
**Function address** A(F): the address of F in the driver's comparison link (§4.4).
**Abstract object**, **slot**, **value set**: §5. ⊤ is the unbounded value set.
**Descriptor**: the in-memory oracle interface record of §8.1.
**Binding**: one parameter or device entry of a descriptor.
**Shape**: a tuple of binding kinds, modes and widths (§8.4).
**Budget record**: the in-memory record `bennett_budget` of §9.1.
**Budget table**: the driver input of §9.2.
**Coherence state**: Cl (classical) or Co (coherent) of a value or object instance (§10, TDL-2).
**Coherent slice**: an outlined maximal region of Co instructions (TDL-3).
**Arena**: the coherent memory of §10 TDL-4.
**Generation**: the classical execution of an action region that records its events (§18.4).
**Device model**: one of `console`, `clock`, `entropy`, `block` (ISA §7.3), realised per tier by §11.

**Coverage classes** (ISA §13): **lowered** (the construct has an ISA realisation), **shimmed** (it is replaced by a runtime or platform shim with a recorded `shim_hash`), **trapped** (it faults with code 8, `FAULT_EFFECT_UNMODELLED`, on the executions that reach it, and has a coverage line).
**Driver mode**: one of the invocation modes of §19.2–§19.7.
**Platform profile**: §20.
**Materialised module**: the module after normalisation (§12).
**Reference object**: the ISA object the map produces for one oracle shape (§16.2); its oracle `@ref` defines F_B.
**Blocker**: a capability with no ISA 0.8 realisation in a stated case (§25.1), BLK-1, BLK-2, BLK-4 and BLK-5 (BLK-3 retired, §25.1).
Every function or global name that starts with `__bennett_` is reserved.
The reserved names other than the markers of §3.2 are:
`__bennett_nz_` | nobody: **primitives**, lowered by the map (§16.4) and the CC/R lowering (§17.4) | the normaliser (§12) and runtimes bitcode
`__bennett_sf_` | `bennett-arith` bitcode (§13) | the normaliser and runtimes bitcode

`__bennett_rt_` | `bennett-runtimes` bitcode (§11, §14, §17, §20); the driver's layout objects `__bennett_rt_blk.<f>` (§14.9) | the normaliser, the driver's synthesised code (§19) and runtimes bitcode
`__bennett_dev_` | `bennett-runtimes` bitcode: device-model entry points and device state (§11.3) | the plugin's L lowering of effect markers and runtimes bitcode
The primitives are exactly:

```
declare void @__bennett_nz_fault(i64 %code)    ; fault with code C (§12.3)
declare ptr  @__bennett_nz_alloc(i64 %n)       ; ISA alloc / lift.alloc (§17.1)
declare void @__bennett_nz_free(ptr %p)        ; ISA free / lift.free
```
A **producer input** is a bitcode file given to the driver other than `bennett-runtimes` and `bennett-arith` bitcode.
A producer input:
MUST NOT define (`define`) a function whose name is a marker or a reserved name (`BD-E-MARKER-DEFINED`);
MUST NOT declare, define or reference a reserved name that is not a marker (`BD-E-MARKER-UNKNOWN`);
MUST NOT use a marker other than as the callee of a call or invoke (`BD-E-MARKER-ADDRESS`): no stored, compared, passed or cast marker address, so that no marker is ever called indirectly.
The driver checks rules 1–3 on every producer input before linking; the plugin checks rules 1 and 3 on the linked module, and, in closed-unit mode (§19.7), all three on its input.
Checked examples are producer inputs.
`__bennett_ctrl_v`, the variadic probe of the spike ABI v0, is not a marker; it is rejected by rule 2.
*(non-normative)* The legality corpus's trace runtime defines markers; it is a test harness, never a production link input (§19.9).
The normative IR signatures (return type, name, parameter types; parameter names are documentation):

Operand roles, by marker (positions are 0-based).
"Dispatched" operands are classical values whose value set (§5.3) selects among compiled alternatives (§3.4); "memory" operands point into classical memory.
`qalloc`, `qborrow` | – | – | 0 `cls`, 1 `n` | – | – | –
`gate` | 1 | – | 0 `op` | – | – | 2 index
`rot` | 1 | – | 0 `op` | – | – | 2 index, 3 angle
`measure` | 0 | – | – | – | – | 1 index
`qprep` | 0 | – | – | – | – | 1 memory (source bytes), 2 byte count
`observe` | – | – | – | – | – | 0 memory, 1 byte count
`ctrl` | 0 | 2 (action) | – | 3 | – | 1 index, 4 env
`adj` | – | 0 (action) | – | 1 | – | 2 env
`compute` | – | 0, 1 (action) | – | 2 | – | 3 env
`reversible` | – | 0 (reversible) | – | 1 | – | 2 env
`oracle` | (in the descriptor) | 0 (oracle) | – | 1 | 2 | –
`inplace` | (in the descriptor) | 0, 1 (oracle) | – | 2 | 3 | –
`effect_console_write` | – | – | – | – | – | 0 memory, 1 length
`effect_clock_read` | – | – | – | – | – | 0 memory (8 bytes)
`effect_entropy_read` | – | – | – | – | – | 0 memory, 1 length
`effect_block_read`, `effect_block_write` | – | – | – | – | – | 0 sector, 1 memory (512 bytes)

Changes from 0.1 and from the spike ABI v0 (`corpus/legality/markers.h`): `qalloc`, `qborrow`, `qfree`, `gate`, `gate2`, `rot`, `measure`, `qload` and `qstore` keep their v0 signatures, so the spike evidence applies to them unchanged; `gate3` is unchanged from 0.1; every region-entry marker now takes a budget record (§9.1); `oracle` and `inplace` take a descriptor (§8.1) in place of 0.1's handle operands; `qprep`, `observe` and the five effect markers are new.

The positive legality requirement (§3.6) is a property of unknown external calls, not of a signature, but every changed or new marker gets legality corpus cases before this version freezes (§21.2, bd `-566`).
**Meaning in brief** (the rules are in the sections named):
`qprep(h, src, n)`: for every k < n and j < 8, wire 8k + j of h ⊕= bit j of byte `src[k]`; n ≤ n(h)/8 (else `T-SIZE`).
A copy when h is clean; self-inverse.
It is how data "fixed classically before entry" (NS §4.2, §8 rung 4) reaches a register (§8.5, §17.4); one `gate` per set bit would need about 1.3·10^8 marker calls for the rung-4 image.

`observe(p, len)`: a computational-basis measurement of the classical bytes [p, p + len) whose coherence state is Co (§10, TDL-11); partial observation retains authoritative basis cells in Co until full coverage permits Cl.
It is the only way superposed classical memory reaches classical code (NS §4.2: "outputs leave through measurement after exit").
On Cl bytes it does nothing.
the effect markers: one per ISA device-model operation (ISA §7.3), realised per tier by §11.
`bennett-runtimes` calls them from its musl, Julia and platform shims; ordinary programs may call them directly.
`spec/bennett_markers.h` is the normative C and C++ header.
Its prototypes (in C++ each carries `noexcept`, which makes clang add `nounwind`, a permitted attribute, and emit `call` rather than `invoke`):
The header also defines:
`typedef struct bennett_q_opaque *bennett_q;` and `typedef void (*bennett_region)(void *env);`;

`bennett_budget` (§9.1), `bennett_bind`, `bennett_devbind` and `bennett_oracle_desc` (§8.1), and the macros `BENNETT_ORACLE_DESC(NP, ND)`, `BENNETT_ORACLE_DESC_P(NP)` and `BENNETT_ORACLE_DESC_D(ND)` that declare a descriptor with NP ≥ 1 parameter bindings and ND ≥ 1 device bindings, parameters only, or devices only;

`bennett_oracle_desc_init(d, np, nd, tgt, fault)` and `bennett_bind_set(b, kind, mode, q, value, size)`, macros that set the fields by plain stores, so that producers build descriptors by constant stores (§8.1);
the operation codes of §3.4 and the constants of §8 and §9.
Clang lowers C `bool` to `zeroext i1`, which §3.6 admits.
The checker compiles the header with clang 18, 20 and 23 and compares every prototype's IR signature with §3.2.
**Operation codes** (`op`):
`gate` | 1 | X | `x`
`gate` | 2 | H | `h`
`gate` | 3 | S | `s`
`gate` | 4 | S† | `sdg`
`gate` | 5 | T | `t`
`gate` | 6 | T† | `tdg`
`gate` | 7 | Z | `s` then `s` (S² = Z exactly)
`gate` | 8 | Y | `sdg` then `x` then `s` (S·X·S† = Y exactly)
`gate2` | 1 | CX, `a` control, `b` target | `cx`
`gate2` | 2 | CZ | `cz`
`gate2` | 3 | SWAP | `swap`
`gate3` | 1 | CCX, `a`, `b` controls, `c` target | `ccx`
`rot` | 1 | RX(θ) | `rx θ`
`rot` | 2 | RY(θ) | `ry θ`
`rot` | 3 | RZ(θ) | `rz θ`
"Then" is time order.
The realisations are exact including global phase, so Z and Y stay exact under control.
**Classes** (`cls`). `cls` = 0 denotes the ISA class `any` (ISA §4.3).

`cls` = k ≥ 1 denotes entry k (1-based) of the link's **class-name table**: the names of the module flags `!"bennett.classes"` (behaviour `AppendUnique`, a list of strings) of every input, in order of first appearance in the driver's link order, followed by the names given with `--bennett-class=<name>` (§19.9) that are not already present.

The driver writes the table into the object's class references (ISA §4.3 `qalloc cls n`, §3.3 `qreg.new cls n`); a name the target does not declare is an ISA load error (ISA §8.3 `classes`), not a dialect error.
**Width** (`n`): the number of qubits, ≥ 1.

statements.text: **Indices**: classical values; an index ≥ n(h) traps (`T-INDEX`, §18.3).
**Angle**: a classical `double` (soft-float bits, §13); a non-finite angle traps (`T-THETA`).
**Constant and run-time operands.** A dispatched operand (role table, §3.2) is classical data.
Its value set VS(v) is computed by §5.3.
The plugin compiles one alternative per member of the **dispatch domain** and selects among them at run time with the compare tree of §14.2:
`op`: the dispatch domain is VS(op) when it is finite, else the marker's whole code table.
A run-time value outside the table traps (`T-OP`).
`cls`: VS(cls) when finite, else {0} ∪ every index of the class-name table.
A value outside traps (`T-CLASS`).
`n`: VS(n) when finite (constants, bounds established by materialised instructions, masks, `select`, `phi`, loads from constant tables, §5.3).
A value 0 at run time traps (`T-SIZE`).
When VS(n) is ⊤, ISA 0.8 has no register of run-time width: the verdict is `blocked:BD-B-ISA4` (BLK-1, §25.1) and the blocker report names the value.

A **constant** operand outside its table (an `op` code not in the table, a constant `cls` beyond the class-name table, a constant `n` = 0) is `BD-E-OPERAND`: the program traps at that marker on every execution that reaches it, so the rejection is fail-fast for an always-failing call (§22.1).
Under coherent control (a Co operand, §10 TDL-10) the same domains apply.

The `cfg-switch-op-table` shape (`default<O3>` sinks seven gate calls into one with a phi of operation codes) is accepted, as are operation codes loaded from a constant table (SimplifyCFG's switch-to-lookup on the `op` operand):

```llvm example=operand-phi-codes verdict=accept
define void @top(i1 %c) {
entry:
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  br i1 %c, label %a, label %b

a:
  br label %j

b:
  br label %j

j:
  %op = phi i32 [ 2, %a ], [ 7, %b ]
  call void @__bennett_gate(i32 %op, ptr %h, i64 0)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}
```

```llvm example=operand-code-table verdict=accept
@switch.table.ops = private unnamed_addr constant [3 x i32] [i32 1, i32 2, i32 5]

define void @top(i64 %i) {
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  %k = urem i64 %i, 3
  %p = getelementptr [3 x i32], ptr @switch.table.ops, i64 0, i64 %k
  %op = load i32, ptr %p
  call void @__bennett_gate(i32 %op, ptr %h, i64 0)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}
```

A call or invoke instruction is a **marker call** iff its callee operand is the function itself (not a loaded or cast value) and that function's name is exactly a marker name.
Names are compared byte for byte; no prefix, suffix or demangled match is made.
A marker call is accepted iff all of the following hold; otherwise `BD-E-MARKER-SIGNATURE`:

the declaration's function type is exactly the marker's IR signature, **or** is the unprototyped form `R (...)` with R the marker's return type (a C declaration without a prototype, spike case `c-unprototyped-decl`);
the call instruction's function type is exactly the marker's IR signature, **or**, only when the declaration is unprototyped, the marker's parameter list followed by `...`;
the call passes exactly as many arguments as the signature has parameters;
the calling convention is the default C convention and the call has no operand bundles.
Attributes and metadata are not part of the comparison; they are governed by §3.6.

```llvm example=recog-unprototyped verdict=accept
declare ptr @__bennett_qalloc(...)
declare void @__bennett_gate(...)
declare void @__bennett_qfree(...)

define void @kr() {
  %h = call ptr (i64, i64, ...) @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  call void (i32, ptr, i64, ...) @__bennett_gate(i32 2, ptr %h, i64 0)
  call void (ptr, ...) @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}
```
The same program passing an `int` index without a cast gives an `i32` argument and is rejected:

```llvm example=recog-unprototyped-wrong-type verdict=reject:BD-E-MARKER-SIGNATURE
declare void @__bennett_gate(...)
declare void @__bennett_qfree(...)

define void @kr() {

  call void (i32, ptr, i32, ...) @__bennett_gate(i32 2, ptr %h, i32 0)
  call void (ptr, ...) @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void
}
```

```llvm example=recog-measure-i8 verdict=reject:BD-E-MARKER-SIGNATURE
declare i8 @__bennett_measure(ptr, i64)

define i8 @m() {
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  %b = call i8 @__bennett_measure(ptr %h, i64 0)
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret i8 %b
}
```

A marker is an external declaration that may read and write any memory, may unwind and may not return: exactly an unknown external function to LLVM.

Stock passes then preserve the dynamic sequence of marker calls on every executed path (spike findings §1: every standard pipeline of LLVM 18, 20 and 23, all 50 legal cases; the four negative controls are detected).
No attribute is needed and none may be added that licenses elimination, commoning, speculation or motion.
Every attribute, keyword and calling convention on a marker declaration or marker call site is in exactly one of three lists:

**Forbidden** (`BD-E-MARKER-ATTRIBUTE`): attributes that license motion or elimination: `memory(...)` in any form, `readnone`, `readonly`, `writeonly`, `argmemonly`, `inaccessiblememonly`, `inaccessiblemem_or_argmemonly`, `willreturn`, `speculatable`, `noreturn`, `returned`, `nocapture`, `captures(...)`, `dereferenceable(...)`, `dereferenceable_or_null(...)`, `align`, `nofpclass(...)`, `byval`, `sret`, `writable`, `initializes(...)`, `dead_on_unwind`, `nosync`, `nofree`, `norecurse`, `mustprogress`, `musttail`, any non-default calling convention, `extern_weak` linkage.

*(non-normative)* The first eight are the spike's L2 forbidden set; `noreturn` would delete the code after a marker; `returned` would replace a marker result by an argument; the parameter-effect attributes would let LLVM move stores to an environment across a region call; `dereferenceable` would let it speculate loads through a handle.

**Benign** (ignored): function position `nounwind`, `nonlazybind`, `uwtable` (any form), `strictfp`, `cold`, `hot`, `nomerge`, `noinline`, `convergent`, `builtin`, `nobuiltin`, `optsize`, `minsize`, `optnone`, and every string attribute; return and parameter position `noundef`, `nonnull`, `range(...)`, `zeroext`, `signext`; declaration linkage and keywords external linkage, `dso_local`, `dso_preemptable`, `unnamed_addr`, `local_unnamed_addr`, any visibility; call-site keywords `tail`, `notail`; instruction metadata of any kind.

The first group is the spike's L2 evidence (findings §1, §4: front ends add `nounwind`, `nonlazybind`, `uwtable`, `noundef`, `nonnull`, `zeroext` and string attributes; passes add `local_unnamed_addr`, `nonnull`, `noundef`, `range`, `tail`).

`strictfp` through `optnone` are added by build flags NS §0 allows (`-ffp-model=strict`, `-Os`, `-O0`) or restrict motion; none licenses elimination, commoning, speculation or motion of an unknown call.
Before this version freezes, a corpus run confirms each of them on the three majors (§21.2, bd `.21`).
**Unknown**: every other attribute is `BD-E-MARKER-ATTRIBUTE` until corpus evidence moves it to one of the lists above with a version change.
This is required by NS §3.1 (the positive legality requirement: an attribute the dialect has not classified may license motion).
Attribute groups (`#N`) are resolved before the check.
Call sites under `-ffp-model=strict` carry `strictfp`; a `cold` declaration is benign too:
Markers never unwind.

Before any other analysis (§4.1 step S1) the plugin rewrites every `invoke` of a marker into a `call` with the same operands followed by `br label %normal`, removes the invoking block from the phi nodes of the unwind destination, and then deletes every block not reachable from the function's entry.
*(non-normative)* This is Enzyme's practice (enzyme survey §1.1); C++ with `-fexceptions` and Rust `extern "C-unwind"` produce such invokes (emission summary item 3).
Front ends SHOULD declare markers non-unwinding (`noexcept`, Rust `extern "C"`).
Unwinding through every other call of device code is the explicit-propagation transform of §14.4; 0.1's `BD-E-EH` is deleted.

```llvm example=unwind-invoke verdict=accept
declare i32 @__gxx_personality_v0(...)

define void @eh() personality ptr @__gxx_personality_v0 {
entry:
  %h = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  invoke void @__bennett_gate(i32 2, ptr %h, i64 0)
          to label %ok unwind label %lp

ok:
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h)
  ret void

lp:
  %e = landingpad { ptr, i32 } cleanup
  resume { ptr, i32 } %e
}
```
**clang (C, C++)** and **rustc** emit markers as direct calls to the declaration (emission summary).
Rust MUST declare each marker with one ABI per crate (`extern "C"`); mixed `"C"`/`"C-unwind"` declarations are merged by rustc into one declaration with `invoke` call sites, which §3.7 accepts.
**Julia** MUST emit markers with `ccall("extern __bennett_<name>", llvmcall, …)` or with `Base.llvmcall((module_ir, "entry"), …)` whose module contains the `declare`.

Both give a direct call to an attribute-free declaration; `ccall("extern __bennett_measure", llvmcall, Bool, …)` gives `declare i1 @__bennett_measure(ptr, i64)`, exactly the §3.2 signature (verified with Julia 1.13.3).
A plain `ccall(:__bennett_x, …)` or `@ccall` is an indirect call through a `jlplt` GOT global and is not a marker call.

The plugin MUST reject a module containing a global variable whose name matches `jlplt___bennett_<name>_<digits>_got` or that carries the attribute `"julia.fname"="__bennett_<name>"` (`BD-E-JULIA-CCALL`), so that this mistake fails at compile time instead of at a lazy binding at run time; the `llvmcall` route keeps the full capability (audit B-13, L).
**Region functions** are passed as `ptr @f` or as any value whose value set §7.2 resolves.
Bennett.jl emits `ptr @f` in its own module (LLVM.jl), which keeps the full capability (audit B-14).

A Julia `@cfunction` pointer is an `inttoptr` constant of an address of the Julia process; like every region pointer with value set ⊤ it is dispatched by value against the address-taken functions of the required type (§7.2), and an execution on which it equals no A(F) traps (`T-REGION`).

**Descriptors and budget records** are built by plain stores into an `alloca` or global (C: the header macros; Rust: `#[repr(C)]` structs; Julia: `Ref` of an `isbits` struct), which survive `default<O3>` as constant stores that §5.3 reads (corpus cases, §21.2).

**Source effect lies** (spike F5). A device function definition carrying any of `memory(none)`, `memory(read)` (any `memory(...)` whose effects exclude a write to any location), `readnone`, `readonly`, `willreturn` or `speculatable`, from which a marker call is reachable through the call graph of §4.1 (the function itself included), is `BD-E-EFFECT-LIE`.

*(non-normative)* LLVM cannot infer these attributes for a function that reaches an unknown external call, so they come from the source; the front end's own optimiser may already have deleted marker calls on their strength, which is why this is a diagnostic and not a guarantee (definedness assumption, NS §3.2).
A plugin processes the whole-program module (after the driver's link and post-link pipeline, §19.1) in this order; the first failing rule gives the verdict (§1.6):
S1 | §3.1 reserved names; §3.5 recognition; §3.6 attributes; §3.8 Julia check; §3.7 marker invokes; §3.8 effect lies; §19.9 version checks
S2 | the device analysis (§5): one fixpoint for points-to, value sets, region candidates (§7.2), indirect-call candidates (§14.2), handle provenance (§6.2) and descriptor kinds (§8.4)
S3 | tier assignment and variants (§4.2–§4.4); calls out of the device program (§4.5)
S4 | handle rules (§6)
S5 | region well-formedness (§7.5)
S6 | the TDL partition and the may-Co analysis (§10)
S7 | normalisation of every device variant (§12) and the residual-poison validator (§12.4); dispatch domains (§3.4)
S8 | lifting (§16) of every oracle shape and coherent slice; in-place verification (§8.7)
S9 | lowering to ISA objects (§17; plugin-defined, constrained by §18.7); blocker reports (§25.1)
Within a step, rules apply in the order listed; within a rule, to instructions in module text order.
Blocker reports are collected during S2–S8 and issued in S9 in that order.

The **call graph** has an edge F → G when F contains a direct `call` or `invoke` of G (after resolving aliases), an edge F → R for every candidate R of every region operand of a marker call in F (a **region edge**), and an edge F → C for every candidate C of every indirect call in F (§14.2).
Only functions with a definition are nodes.
The **closure** of a function is the set of functions reachable from it by direct and indirect-candidate edges (region edges start a new region and are not followed).
Every defined function reachable from the program's roots gets a set of tiers.
The **host roots** are the functions with non-local linkage and the functions whose address host code uses; the **device roots** are the region candidates and the whole-program entry of §19.2.

**CC**: a function that contains a marker call, receives a handle (a parameter or a loaded value whose provenance contains a root, §6.2), is a candidate of an action region operand (its classical part is the generation, §18.4), is a device entry, is in the CC closure of one of these, or is promoted by §19.4.
**R**: a function in the closure of a `reversible` region operand, or every function under `--bennett-tier=reversible` (§19.2).
**L**: a function in the closure of an oracle or in-place region operand, or of a coherent slice (§10, TDL-3).
**H**: every other function reachable from a host root, and every function reachable from a host root through host code only.
A function in no device tier stays H only.
A function may get several tiers; it then has one variant per tier (§4.3).
*(non-normative)* SQLite in the rung-4 program is H (the host builds and serialises the database) and L (the oracle runs the query), so it has two variants and one set of globals (SQLite §5.2(i)).

A **variant** is a (function, tier, coherence signature) triple, where the coherence signature is the tuple of coherence states of the function's parameters and of the may-Co objects it reads (§10, TDL-2) and is empty outside TDL.
The H variant is the original function; every device variant is a clone.
**Clones share every global: data is never cloned.**
There is one classical memory (NS §3.2), shared by H, CC, R and the entry state of every L invocation (§8.5).
Calls inside a variant call the variant of the callee with the caller's tier and the coherence signature at the call.
0.1's `BD-E-DEVICE-ADDRESS` is deleted: a host function may take the address of any function (audit B-16).

Every function whose address is used has the **function address** A(F): its address in the driver's **comparison link** (§19.5: non-PIE, fixed section addresses, identical-code folding and constant merging off; NS §3.2, SQLite §5.2(ii)).
A(F) is the value of `ptr @F` in every tier:
in host code, by linking the production host image with the comparison layout whenever an address may cross the host–device boundary (§19.5);
in CC and R code, as `const` plus `inttoptr` (ISA §4.1);
in lifted code, as `lift.const` (ISA §4.2);
in every data image: global initialisers, vtables, function tables (SQLite's `aBuiltinFunc`, VFS and pcache method tables).
So `ptrtoint`, comparison, hashing and storage of function pointers equal native execution.

statements.text: Each tier maps A(F) to its own variant of F by the dispatch of §14.2.
Two functions never have equal A(F) (identical-code folding is off), so the map is well defined.
A `blockaddress` constant is §14.9.
A call in a device variant of a function with no definition resolves, in this order:
a marker (§3.2) or a primitive (§3.1);

a **runtime shim**: a definition of the symbol in `bennett-runtimes` or `bennett-arith` bitcode, which the driver links before S2 (§19.1): libc and libm (musl-derived), libpthread with one thread, the Julia shim runtime, Rust's `core::panicking::*` targets and the platform shims of §20.
The shim is an ordinary device function (coverage class `shimmed`, with its `shim_hash`, ISA §13);
in a CC variant only, a **host call** through `hostcall` (§11.4);
otherwise **trapped**: the call is replaced by F(8) (§12.3) and the coverage report has a `trapped` line for it (NS §3.3: "Calls with no bitcode are coverage-report lines (*trapped*), never silent").
An R or L variant never makes a host call (ISA §4.1: `hostcall` is CC only; NS §4.2: coherent regions are closed).
*(non-normative)* Item 4 is the only fault the dialect introduces for a call, and it occurs only on the executions that reach the call; it is the north star's own rule.

The device analysis is a whole-program, flow-insensitive, inclusion-based (Andersen-style), field-sensitive points-to and value-set analysis over every device variant and every host function that exchanges data with one (passes it a pointer, or shares a global it accesses).
It is specified exactly: **every verdict, candidate set and dispatch domain of this document is computed from the reference analysis below.**

A plugin MAY use a more precise analysis to shrink dispatch domains or arena placement in its lowering, never to change a verdict (the run-time value is always a member of the reference set, so the results are unchanged).
The **abstract objects** are:
each `alloca` instruction;
each global variable;

each **allocation site**: a call of a function that carries `allockind("alloc")` or `allocsize(...)`, or whose name is one of `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `aligned_alloc`, `posix_memalign` (the object is the one written through its first argument), `memalign`, `strdup`, `strndup`, `_Znwm`, `_Znam`, `_ZnwmRKSt9nothrow_t`, `_ZnamRKSt9nothrow_t`, `_ZnwmSt11align_val_t`, `_ZnamSt11align_val_t`, `__rust_alloc`, `__rust_alloc_zeroed`, `__rust_realloc`, `julia.gc_alloc_obj`, `ijl_gc_alloc_typed`, `jl_gc_alloc`, `ijl_gc_small_alloc`, `ijl_gc_big_alloc`, or `__bennett_nz_alloc`;
the pseudo-object `EXT` (memory of unknown provenance: host memory reached through a pointer the analysis did not create).
Heap objects are context-insensitive: one object per allocation-site instruction of the variant in which it occurs.
The list above is the reference list; `bennett-runtimes` declares its allocator entry points with `allockind("alloc")` so that they are covered by the first rule.
An **offset** is an integer byte offset, a **residue class** (r mod s)[lo, hi) with s ≥ 2 (every offset o with o ≡ r (mod s) and lo ≤ o < hi), or `*` (any offset).
An **atom** is one of:
`(X, o)`: a pointer into object X at offset o;
`FN(F)`: the address A(F) of a defined function F;
`ROOT(r)`: a handle with root r (the allocation site of a `qalloc`/`qborrow` call, §6.5);
`INT(c)`: the integer constant c (of the value's width).

Every SSA value v (per lane for vectors, per index path for aggregates) has an **abstract value** AV(v) = (A, t): a finite set A of atoms and a flag t; t = ⊤ means "and any other integer or address". ⊤ never stands for a `ROOT` atom (handle provenance is always explicit); for a function-pointer operand it stands for "any function of the operand's type whose address is used" (§7.2, §14.2).
Every slot (X, o) of memory has a content AV(X, o) of the same form.
When A holds more than **K = 4096** `INT` atoms they are dropped and t is set (a normative constant: it decides dispatch and blocker verdicts, so §24 does not defer it).
"AV(v) = ⊤" below means t is set; unions and inclusions are taken component-wise.
Before the fixpoint, seed the initialiser atoms of every global, mutable or constant, into its slots.
statements.uncertain: no RFC keyword, defined term, example marker or declarative verb

statements.text: For each alloca and allocation-site object, also represent every extent whose initial contents are zero under §§17.1/17.3 as a zero-byte initial image; represent a nonconstant extent symbolically over its possible allocated bytes.
Subsequent stores union additional possibilities and never erase these initial possibilities.
This is an initial image, not a claim that the object remains immutable.
The analysis is the least fixpoint of the following rules over AV.
"Copies" means AV(result) ⊇ AV(operand) lane by lane; ⊤ absorbs.

S2 models the value effects of the specified normalisation before verdicts and dispatch domains freeze; pre-normalisation syntax does not permit omitting a value produced by the materialised execution.
PT1 | `alloca`, global `@G`, allocation-site call | AV ∋ (X, 0); zero-filled initial extents are seeded as above

PT2 | `getelementptr T, ptr p, idx…` | uses P(a), I(a) and the complete finite-width computation of §16.4, also for constant expressions: sequential indices are sign-extended/truncated to I(a), scaling and offset accumulation wrap modulo 2^I(a), and addition preserves pointer bits above I(a).
Zero accumulated offset copies AV(p).

For every (X,o), include the image of all represented base addresses and index values (unknown base bits range over patterns consistent with DataLayout and X's alignment), using integer/residue-class/`*` offset unions.
Unbounded mathematical addition is not a substitute.
If an address may leave X, include (EXT, `*`) and the non-handle top flag; PT6 propagates this unknown-address alternative.
The unknown-address alternative does not by itself establish host escape (§6.4): retain the original base provenance for that test; actual host/unknown origins keep their restrictions.
ROOT provenance and §6.2 restrictions remain explicit.
Array dimensions determine stride, never an index bound
PT3 | `phi`, `select` (value operands), `freeze`, `addrspacecast`; `bitcast` | the first four copy (union).
A bitcast copies lane by lane only when source and destination have identical lane counts and per-lane representation widths, treating a scalar as one lane.
Otherwise use the virtual N21 bitcast expansion of §12.6: pack source-lane bit patterns into its prescribed bit string in DataLayout order, then resegment at the destination representation width.
Compute output AV through PT4/PT5 transfers of that expansion; finite INT lane sets denote their full Cartesian product, and K applies per resulting lane.
Never copy a source-lane INT atom as the value of a packed destination scalar.
Unknown bits propagate non-handle top through those transfers.
Explicit object and ROOT provenance follows the same expansion and remains subject to §6.2; top never substitutes for ROOT.
Apply also to constant expressions and fixed-vscale forms during S2 before verdicts, candidate sets, shapes and dispatch domains freeze.
Direct finite bit-string evaluation is equivalent; no LLVM optimisation is required
PT4 | `ptrtoint`, `inttoptr`, `zext`/`sext`/`trunc` | copy only bit-preserving conversions.
Otherwise apply the actual source/destination-width bit-vector conversion (§16.4): ptrtoint/inttoptr zero-extend or truncate at P(a), sext sign-extends.
Use PT2’s represented-address image construction, retaining originating object and ROOT provenance.
A narrowed representation that cannot be reassociated with its original object adds (EXT, `*`) and non-handle ⊤; numerical uncertainty is not host escape.
Apply also to constant expressions
PT5 | `add`/`sub` of a value with pointer atoms and an `INT` set | computes address bits modulo 2^W at the integer operation’s width W, never unbounded offset addition.
Relative displacements from the originating base are modular too: zero net displacement represents that base again, including after an inttoptr truncation to P(a).
Use PT2’s represented-address image construction at W bits (full-width arithmetic, no preserved high GEP bits), retaining original object and ROOT provenance.
Keep modular displacement alternatives even outside the allocation, and additionally include (EXT, `*`) and non-handle ⊤ when an image may leave it.
Residue classes and `*` take the same finite-width image; an unrepresentable image retains (X, `*`) for each originating X plus (EXT, `*`) and non-handle ⊤.
Other integer operations on pointer atoms use that conservative image.
Widening a pointer-derived integer by zext/sext uses that conservative image too (fixed reference fallback); ptrtoint zero-extension retains its base representation.
Numerical uncertainty does not itself establish host escape (PT2).

The rules apply also to constant expressions, before candidate/dispatch domains freeze; on finite `INT` sets, every LLVM integer operation, cast and `icmp` is evaluated elementwise; with x ⊤ and a constant m, `and x, m` gives the submasks of m and `urem x, m` gives {0, …, m−1} (each still subject to K); a range attribute or `!range` metadata removed by N3/N4 is not a bound on materialised execution and MUST NOT restrict any verdict, candidate set, descriptor shape or dispatch domain.
Only bounds independently established by materialised instructions restrict the set; otherwise retain ⊤ and apply the ordinary operation rules, including finite masks/remainders

PT6 | `load T, ptr p` | for each (X,o) ∈ AV(p): memory atoms carry their storage interval and representation width; copy a whole-value atom only for that identical interval with a compatible representation.
A known immutable byte image decodes exactly the accessed bytes using DataLayout and T (including initialisers).
For a partial, spanning or overlapping access whose result bits are not represented exactly, the non-handle value is ⊤, never the union of component INT values.
X=EXT gives ⊤.
A non-handle top flag on p contributes the same unknown-address load alternative even when explicit object offsets overlap no known slot; it MUST NOT be dropped.
ROOT provenance remains explicit and §6.2's partial-handle restrictions still apply.

For a possibly valid load wholly contained in a zero-filled initial extent, include the all-zero value of the load’s representation and width, unioned with values from every overlapping store or copy under these interval rules.
PT8 propagates these initial byte possibilities when copying memory.
Zero contributes no ROOT.
Region inputs, replayed caller bytes and other nonzero-initialised contents retain their specified sources; this rule does not replace them with zeros
PT7 | `store v, ptr p` | retain each written interval and representation width; partial writes overlapping a larger load participate in PT6's conservative fallback.
AV(X, o + d_k) ⊇ AV(v_k) for each (X, o) ∈ AV(p) and each lane or field k at byte offset d_k

PT8 | memory copy (`llvm.memcpy`/`memmove`/`memcpy.inline`, `__bennett_rt_memmove`) of (dst, src, len); memory fill (`llvm.memset`, `__bennett_rt_memset`) of (dst, v, len) | copy: propagate zero-byte initial images over the copied byte ranges, including their symbolic extents; for each slot (Y, s) of each (Y, o_s) ∈ AV(src) and (Z, o_d) ∈ AV(dst): when offsets and len are constants and the atom's entire storage interval [s, s + size(atom)) lies in the copied range, copy its atom and representation width to (Z, o_d + s − o_s).
Every partially overlapping atom instead contributes non-handle ⊤ and explicit ROOT provenance to the affected destination interval (unknown offsets/len use `*`); do not copy the whole component INT.

Fill: every slot in [o_d, o_d + len) of each (Z, o_d) ∈ AV(dst) (all of Z when an offset or len is not constant) gets the `INT` atoms of the byte v repeated to the slot's width (⊤ when v is not constant)

PT9 | direct call of G, or indirect call with candidate G (§14.2) | AV(parameter i of G) ⊇ AV(argument i); AV(result) ⊇ the union of AV over G's `ret` operands; `byval` arguments copy the pointee's slots into the callee's copy object
PT10 | `insertelement`/`extractelement`/`shufflevector`/`insertvalue`/`extractvalue` | extraction/insertion use N15’s total unsigned index semantics.
Constant in-range extraction copies its lane; constant out-of-range extraction gives the element type’s zero.
Dynamic extraction unions every source lane selected by a represented index, plus zero iff the index set includes an unsigned value >= L (including top when 2^K > L).
No zero is added if every represented index is in range; zero adds no ROOT.
In-range insertion replaces the selected lane; out-of-range insertion preserves the vector.
Dynamic insertion includes each old lane unless it is certainly replaced, and the inserted value whenever that lane can be selected.
Valid shuffle indices and aggregate paths move atoms unchanged (handle-table reads, audit B-23)

PT11 | a parameter of a function with a host caller, a device entry, or a function whose address host code uses | AV ⊇ {(EXT, `*`)} for `ptr` parameters, ⊤ for integer parameters, plus the atoms of the device-side arguments by PT9; for a pointer parameter i of a device entry E, also the candidate atom ROOT(E, i) of §6.6

PT12 | a `qalloc`/`qborrow` call; a call of a function with no definition that resolves to a host call (§4.5) or is trapped; an `atomicrmw`/`cmpxchg` (before N9) | `qalloc`/`qborrow`: AV ∋ ROOT(site) (§6.5).
An undefined callee: the result is ⊤ and every slot reachable from its pointer arguments gets ⊤.
`atomicrmw`/`cmpxchg`: a load plus a store (PT6, PT7)

An `inttoptr` of a constant gives (EXT, `*`) and, for function-pointer purposes, ⊤: function addresses are symbolic `FN` atoms during the analysis, and their numeric values A(F) are fixed only by the comparison link (§19.5), after normalisation (S7) and before lifting (S8).
PT12 checked ROOT propagation: `make` returns the fresh qalloc ROOT to its caller; the caller uses that same identity for a gate and free.
This is a direct handle realisation, so no stored-instance bound is required.
The checked verdict is accept.
**Zero initial images (DB/DN/DS).** Before any conditional store, the stack allocation's eight bytes are zero under N24.
The path storing 1 adds a second possibility, so AV(raw)=AV(idx)={INT(0),INT(1)} and VS(width)={1,3}.
The heap companion uses a zero-filled calloc allocation-site object with the same derivation.
The PT8 companion copies the stack image to a mutable global whose initial value is 1: zero must come from the source, not the destination.
All accept.
LLVM 18/23 verify source O0; N24/N8/N15/N21 materialisation and native O0/O3 runs for false/true observe widths 1/3, one clean free each, live_after=0 and code 0.
Source uninitialised LLVM loads are not execution oracles; the comparison executes the specified zero-filled materialised program.

A constant-byte fill carries its complete filled interval and byte value; a load contained in that interval decodes the repeated byte at the load's width.
Other overlapping writes still participate in PT6 (a fill does not erase them).
PT8 copies preserve storage intervals/representation widths only for fully copied atoms.
Partial copies and fills add overlapping affected intervals; PT6 then returns ⊤ for any load whose whole bits are not represented exactly.
These are fixed reference rules, not optional precision improvements.

The **value set** VS(v) of an integer or pointer operand is the set of its `INT` and `FN` atoms (pointer atoms denote addresses that are not compile-time constants and make VS(v) = ⊤ for dispatch purposes), or ⊤.
A value set is a precision tool only:
an operand with a finite VS is dispatched over it (§3.4, §14.2);

an operand with VS = ⊤ is dispatched over its type's whole valid domain where that domain is finite: operation codes and classes (§3.4), binding kinds (§8.4), the function addresses of a type (§7.2, §14.2);
otherwise it is a blocker case of §25.1: widths (BLK-1), budgets computed on the device (BLK-2), parameters of in-place pairs (§8.7).
`FN` atoms of region operands | region candidate sets (§7.2)
`FN` atoms of indirect callees | indirect-call candidate sets (§14.2)
`ROOT` atoms | handle provenance (§6.2), handle containment (§6.4), static register files (§6.5)
`INT` atoms of descriptor and budget fields | descriptor shapes (§8.4), budget pre-minting (§9.5)
slots stored under control | the may-Co analysis and arena placement (§10, TDL-2, TDL-4)
objects loaded by L code | the oracle read set R and entry-state transfer (§8.5)
`INT` atoms of `op`, `cls`, `n` | dispatch domains (§3.4)

```llvm example=pt-variable-index verdict=accept
define void @t(i64 %i) {
  %s = alloca %struct.tab
  %h0 = call ptr @__bennett_qalloc(i64 0, i64 1)
  store ptr %h0, ptr %s
  %pn = getelementptr %struct.tab, ptr %s, i64 0, i32 1
  store i64 3, ptr %pn
  %k = and i64 %i, 3
  %pk = getelementptr %struct.tab, ptr %s, i64 0, i32 0, i64 %k
  %hk = load ptr, ptr %pk
  call void @__bennett_gate(i32 1, ptr %hk, i64 0)
  %n = load i64, ptr %pn
  %n2 = add i64 %n, 1
  store i64 %n2, ptr %pn
  call void @__bennett_qfree(ptr %h0)
  ret void
}
```
*(non-normative)* In `pt-variable-index`, `%pk` has the offset class (0 mod 8)[0, 32) in `%s` (the `[4 x ptr]` array), so the load `%hk` reads the slots 0, 8, 16, 24: AV(`%hk`) = {ROOT(`%h0`)}.

The count field is at the exact offset 32, outside the class, so AV(`%n`) holds INT(3) and, through the store of `%n2`, INT(4), INT(5), … until it exceeds K and becomes ⊤; it holds no `ROOT` atom, and the arithmetic on it is legal (audit B-27: 0.1 gave the load offset `*` and rejected this program).
**Finite-width and materialised-domain witnesses (round 6).** Under I=32, 2^32 truncates to zero, so the table load yields FN(body) and dispatch succeeds.
For the ranged inputs, N3/N4 erase the annotations: `n & 3` gives {0,1,2,3} and `| 1` gives {1,3}.
At n=2 width 3 admits both X gates on wire 2 and a clean free.
No new input precondition or fault is introduced.

A handle is an ordinary `ptr` in address space 0.

In device memory and in integers a handle is its **register tag**: an opaque value below 2^pw assigned to an allocation generation (§6.5), nonzero and distinct from every identity still observable through live or stale copies.
Physical slots are reusable storage, never allocation identity.
A tag MUST NOT be recycled while an observable stale copy can remain; integer wrap is not permission to alias generations.
Copies continue to denote their original generation after free.
ISA 0.8 has no instruction that reads a `qreg`'s launch id (BLK-1's `qreg.id` would add one), so tags are the plugin's.
At the host–device boundary a handle is the ISA launch register id (`bennett_qreg`, ISA §10), which the launch binds to a `qreg` parameter or result (§6.6).
Neither value may influence a result other than through §6.3; the rules below make them unobservable.
A handle denotes a register of n wires, n the `qalloc` operand; wire i of handle h is written h.i.
The **provenance** of a value is the set of `ROOT` atoms of its abstract value (§5).

Provenance flows through **bitwise copies** only: `ptrtoint`/`inttoptr` at width pw, integer loads and stores of width pw, vector lanes (including dynamic lanes, PT10: a dynamically indexed vector of handles is a handle table), aggregate fields, memory copies, `phi`, `select`, `freeze`, call arguments and returns (PT3–PT10).
A handle-derived value (any lane or field) MAY be:
a handle operand of a marker (§3.2);
copied by the rules above, including storage in any slot the analysis tracks (§6.4);
an operand of `icmp eq` or `icmp ne` (§6.3);
an argument of a direct or indirect call of a defined function, or a return value.

Every other use is `BD-E-HANDLE-USE` (maintainer decision 2: "any other use of a handle-derived integer is rejected fail-loud"; NS §3.1 "never dereferenced"): in particular arithmetic, bitwise operations, `icmp` with any other predicate, any cast other than the copies above (`trunc`, `zext`, `sext`, `bitcast` to a non-pointer-width type, `ptrtoint` to a width ≠ pw), `getelementptr` with a handle as base or index, `switch` on it, use as the pointer operand of a `load`, `store`, `atomicrmw`, `cmpxchg` or memory intrinsic (dereference), and a load of any type whose byte range overlaps a handle-derived slot without being exactly one pw-wide lane of it (a partial read).
A handle operand of a marker whose provenance is empty is `BD-E-HANDLE-UNTRACKED` (it cannot be a handle of this program).
*(non-normative)* A tracked value that at run time is not a live handle (a stale copy, a freed register) traps at the marker (`T-DEAD`, §18.3).

`icmp eq` and `icmp ne` of a handle with `null`, or with another handle-derived value, compare **identity**: a live handle is never null, and two handles are equal iff they denote the same allocation generation, including when comparing a freed identity with a later allocation in the same physical slot.
The result is not handle-derived.
In CC it lowers to `icmp` on register tags.
This covers C `if (!q)` and Rust's `Option<Handle>` niche (audit D8).
*(non-normative)* A comparison is a classical observation of identity, not of the register's content; ids are unique, so it equals the native comparison of the two handle values.

Handles may be stored in any slot the analysis tracks: tables, vectors, linked structures, globals (field-sensitively), heap objects, and objects passed to indirect calls or returned by address-taken functions (audit B-22, B-24, B-26, B-29).
A handle may **escape** only where code the analysis cannot see could read it:

`BD-E-HANDLE-ESCAPE`: a `ROOT` atom reaches a slot of `EXT`, an argument or a reachable slot of a call that resolves to a host call or is trapped (§4.5), or the return value of a function whose callers are not all in the link, other than a device entry's `QREG` result (§6.6).
NS §3.1: "any handle use that survives into host native code is rejected".

H functions in the link that receive launch register ids through §6.6 are analysed like device code: they may copy, store, compare and pass them back to device entries (§6.2 items 2–4); any other use is `BD-E-HANDLE-USE`.
ISA 0.8 has no instruction that stores, loads or converts a `qreg` (ISA §3.2, §3.3, §4.1), and `qreg[n]` types have literal widths.
CC code holds `qreg` values in its classical environment (dynamic SSA instances, block parameters, call arguments and results; ISA §3.2, §7.4).
The plugin realises each allocation site s (a `qalloc` or `qborrow` call) in one of two ways:

**Direct.** If no `ROOT(s)` atom reaches a memory slot (PT7, PT8), the handle is a CC `qreg` value threaded through SSA values, block parameters, call arguments and results ("register- environment passing"; §25.2 records that ISA §3.3's transition table should name CC `call`, `ret` and `br` operands of `qreg` type).
Every execution of s creates a new dynamic instance, so loops and recursion need no bound.
**Static register file.** Otherwise a physical **slot** is a pair (s, instance index k < N(s)); ROOT(s) is static provenance, not run-time identity.

For each slot the plugin keeps one CC `qreg` variable, threaded like a direct handle through every CC variant that may use it; `qalloc` at s picks a free instance index at run time and executes `qreg.new cls n` into that variable (one variable per member of the width dispatch domain, §3.4).
The default CC table holds each slot's current generation tag and liveness; a fresh-tag allocator gives every allocation a new identity (§6.1), stored in memory.
A marker operand is dispatched by matching its full tag against current live candidate slots (compare tree, §14.2); a missing or retired generation traps T-DEAD before changing any register.
Free retires the identity even if the slot is immediately reused.
Recycle tags only after old copies are proven unobservable, never by slot reuse alone.
This table and allocator use ordinary classical operations, without qreg.id.
N(s) bounds simultaneous physical slots, not the number of historical identities.
A direct handle that is converted to an integer (`ptrtoint`, a store) gets a tag in the same way.
**Reference instance bound** of a site s in function F with a static register file:

Before rules 1–2, augment each function's CFG with N29 continuation edges: from every call whose closure may longjmp, add an edge to each setjmp continuation in every function that may be an ancestor of that call (including the same function).
Include the materialised __bennett_rt_setjmp continuations, candidate callees and interprocedural call edges.
The reference default remains conservative: if a setjmp continuation in any may-ancestor A of F (A=F included) can reach s through these CFG and call edges, s is not self-disjoint and E(s)=∞.
Apply this rule to §7.5(b) R hoisting as well.
Such a site uses BLK-1 (R hoisting: BLK-4), with the bounded static-file fallback, never rejection.
The read-only ISA 0.9 draft's K1 supplies the exact missing dynamic qreg.width/id/from_id and run-time-width register capability; K2 supplies R allocation for BLK-4.
Neither witness claims a finite reference bound.

**Entry-boundary liveness (before rules 1–2).** If an instance of s may be live at the return of any device entry that may reach s — memory live at that return (a global, heap object, or memory reachable from a result or env) may hold ROOT(s), and not every path from s through the augmented CFGs and call edges to that return passes a qfree with provenance exactly {s} — then s is not self-disjoint and E(s)=∞.
Use BLK-1, with the bounded static-file fallback, never rejection.
The host may call entries any number of times: executions per entry call do not bound instances that survive return.
Under §7.5(b), substitute reversible-invocation return and BLK-4; the same boundary test precedes hoisting.
An internal callee's return alone is not a device-entry return: a guaranteed free in its caller before the entry returns can discharge this condition.
**Parameter and result roots.** Apply the same boundary test to candidate handle parameter ROOT(E,i) (§6.6), and to a qalloc instance returned as an entry QREG result.
Persistent memory (a global, heap object, or memory reachable from result or env) or the entry's QREG result may retain it.
Include every reusable exit, including unwind/resume edges, in the augmented interprocedural graph; an exact-root qfree on every path from receipt/allocation discharges liveness.
Otherwise E=∞: the host may supply or retain unboundedly many distinct live registers across calls.
Marker uses of such roots loaded from persistent memory are BLK-1 blocker points (`blocked:BD-B-ISA4`), with §25.1's bounded static-file fallback and blocker trap, never rejection.
A handle parameter used directly only within its receiving entry keeps the direct realisation, as does a returned QREG never stored in memory.
The infinite bound on a returned root is relevant to its static-file realisation when it reaches memory; it does not impose a finite bound on direct QREG transport.
Under §7.5(b), substitute reversible-invocation exit and BLK-4 (`blocked:BD-B-ISA12`) for receipt through env.

s is **self-disjoint** iff the only memory its `ROOT(s)` atom reaches is allocas of F whose address does not escape F (it is not stored, returned, or passed to a call other than a marker call, which includes the `env` of a region-entry marker), and every CFG path of F from s to a `ret`, to s again, or to a call whose callee may reach F through the call graph passes through a `qfree` whose operand's provenance is exactly {s}.
Then N(s) = 1.

Otherwise N(s) = E(s), the bound on executions of s per device-entry call: E(s) = TC(s) × Σ_c E(c) over the device call sites c of F (E = 1 for a device entry), where TC(s) is the product of the constant maximum trip counts of the loops of F's augmented CFG that contain s (LLVM's `ScalarEvolution::getSmallConstantMaxTripCount` on the materialised module of the major in use), and E(s) = ∞ when a containing loop has no constant maximum trip count or F is in a cycle of the call graph.
E(c), for a call site c in function C, uses the same recurrence: TC(c) in C's augmented CFG times the sum of E over C's device call sites (entry multiplicity 1).
Any unbounded augmented loop, recursive cycle or conservative setjmp-continuation or entry-boundary-liveness case gives infinity; normal CFG loop facts cannot override it.
If N(s) = ∞, every execution of s is a **blocker point** of BLK-1 (`blocked:BD-B-ISA4`, §25.1): ISA 0.8 cannot name an unbounded number of registers reached through memory.
The plugin compiles the program with a static file of `--bennett-qreg-instances` instances (default 64, §24) and a blocker trap (§25.1) on an execution that needs more.

statements.text: `qload(dst, mem, addr)`: XOR of cell `addr` of `mem` into `dst` (§18.3); a copy when `dst` is clean, the source preserved;
`qstore(mem, addr, val)`: XOR of `val` into cell `addr` of `mem` (ISA `qstore`), whatever `mem` holds;
`qprep(h, src, n)`: XOR of classical bytes into `h` (§3.2);
`inplace(g, ginv, budget, desc)`: x ← g(x), admitted only under §8.7;
`oracle(f, budget, desc)`: targets ⊕= outputs, fault ⊕= code, inputs preserved (§8).

The north star's compile-time rule "a store into a register not known to be clean is an error" (NS §3.1) is the optional warning **`BD-W-QSTORE-UNCLEAN`**: under `-bennett-warn-qstore`, the plugin warns at every `qstore` whose target is not provably clean (no event since its `qalloc` other than a `qstore` of the same `addr` and `val`).
The warning never changes the verdict, so the uncomputing second store stays legal (§1.4).
The plugin converts handles to ISA wires (ISA §3.3 linear values) when it lowers.

Its obligations, each a property of every ISA object it emits (ISA suite F), are: every gate's wires pairwise distinct; no wire used after its release; every `qalloc`ed bundle released by an explicit `qfree` (ISA §5.1); every control context disjoint from the operands it controls (ISA §3.3); the uncomputation-validity discipline of ISA §6 for every value it introduces.

Where an obligation depends on run-time data, the reference semantics checks it dynamically and the plugin MUST include the same check (§18.3 traps `T-ALIAS`, `T-DEAD`, `T-LEAK`, `T-CTRL`); `T-CLEAN` is checked as ISA `qreg.free` cleanliness is: by simulating executors, with hardware following ISA §17 item 14.
