F(C): the instruction is replaced by `call void @__bennett_nz_fault(i64 C)` followed by `unreachable`; the instructions after it in its block are deleted, and the block is removed from the incoming lists of the phi nodes of its former successors.

`__bennett_nz_fault` is a primitive (§3.1): `bennett-runtimes` defines it for the native comparison build (record C and end the device entry with fault C); the map gives it the row `fault C` (§16.4); CC and R lower it by §11.5.
The validator inspects the materialised device variants and rejects (`BD-E-RESIDUAL`) any of:
V1 | a flag of N1 or N2
V2 | instruction metadata other than `!dbg` and `!bennett.rstep`
V3 | an attribute N4 removes, on a device function, its parameters or return, or a call site in a device function
V4 | a call of an intrinsic that N0, N5, N6, N10, N11, N16, N21, N24, N26, N27, N32 or N33 removes, or of `llvm.abs`/`ctlz`/`cttz` with a `true` flag
V5 | an `undef` or `poison` constant in a device function or in the initialiser of a global a device function references
V6 | `freeze`, `fence`, `atomicrmw`, `cmpxchg`, an atomic or volatile load or store

V7 | a shift whose amount is not a constant < W, unless the shift's only use is as the false operand of a `select` whose true operand is 0 and whose condition is `icmp uge` of the same amount and the constant W
V8 | `extractelement`/`insertelement` with a non-constant index outside the N15 pattern (only before N21; after N21 no vector remains, V13)

V9 | a floating-point instruction other than `fneg`, `bitcast`, `load`, `store`, `select` and `phi` of a floating-point value, or a call of a floating-point intrinsic other than `llvm.fabs` and `llvm.copysign` (after N32/N33; 0.1's V9 is inverted)

V10 | an operand or result of type `half`, `bfloat`, `x86_fp80`, `fp128` or `ppc_fp128` other than in the bit-exact forms retained by §13.1 (`fneg`, `llvm.fabs`, `llvm.copysign`, `bitcast`, `load`, `store`, `select`, `phi`) or value transport through function parameters, call arguments/results, `ret`, `insertvalue` and `extractvalue` (§16.2–§16.4); calls remain subject to V4, V9 and V12 (after N32/N33)
V11 | an `alloca` (after N24; replaces 0.1's V11)
V12 | in an L or R variant, a call of a function without a definition other than a primitive, a runtime entry point defined in the link, or a trapped call already replaced by F(8)
V13 | a value of vector type
V14 | a value of type iN with N > 128

V15 | `va_start`, `va_end`, `va_copy`, `va_arg`, `invoke`, `landingpad`, `resume`, `cleanuppad`, `catchpad`, `catchswitch`, `cleanupret`, `catchret`, a call of `setjmp`, `_setjmp`, `sigsetjmp` or `__sigsetjmp`
V16 | inline `asm` or a call of a target intrinsic (`llvm.<target>.*`)
The plugin's validator and `bennett-conformance`'s are implemented independently (NS §3.2); a disagreement on any input is a conformance failure of one of them.
Checked validator boundary pairs.
Each positive is materialised IR accepted by the validator, and each negative retains the named forbidden construct (V8 also has V13).
These test validation, not producer acceptance or executable result delivery.
**V2.** Only the permitted R charge metadata remains; the return is not hidden by a poison assumption.
**V3.** The pointer parameter and its load carry no N4 attributes.
**V4.** Both true-flag and false-flag residual count intrinsics are rejected.
The materialised runtime helper defines ctlz(0)=8.

**V9.** fneg double is the explicitly retained bit operation. fadd is arithmetic requiring N32.
**V10.** V10 must permit every bit-exact operation retained by §13.1 and every carrier transport admitted by §16, for all seven floating-point formats.
For `half`, `fneg` maps carrier bits b to b xor 0x8000, preserving NaN payload and quiet/signaling bits; it is not arithmetic to rewrite or reject.
The positive retains it between load and bitcast.
The negative instead retains `fadd half`, which N32 must rewrite to `__bennett_sf_add_f16` on i16 carriers.
The interface witness also retains `llvm.fabs`/`llvm.copysign` and transports a half value through a defined call, return and aggregate; none is a V10 residue.

  %v = load half, ptr %p

A scalable vector type `<vscale x L x T>` has L·V lanes, where V is the constant `vscale` of the link: the function attribute `vscale_range(V, V)` when every device function that uses scalable vectors carries it with equal bounds, else the driver option `--bennett-vscale=<V>` (default: the minimum of the `vscale_range` bounds, §24).
The native comparison build is compiled for the same V (`-msve-vector-bits=128·V` or `-mrvv-vector-bits`).
N10 replaces `llvm.vscale` by V and N21 scalarises the L·V lanes.
*(non-normative)* x86-64 has no scalable vectors; the rule exists so that AArch64 SVE and RISC-V V code is liftable.
For a value `%v` of type `<L x T>`, lane k is the scalar `%nz.l<k>.v` (k = 0 … L − 1).
Rules, in lane order k = 0, 1, …:

elementwise instructions (binary, bitwise, `icmp`, `fcmp`, casts, `select` with a vector or scalar condition, unary `fneg`, `freeze`, calls of elementwise intrinsics): one scalar instruction per lane, `%nz.l<k>.r = <op> T %nz.l<k>.a, %nz.l<k>.b`;
`bitcast` is elementwise only for equal lane geometries.
Otherwise pack the source bit string in datalayout order and resegment it into destination lanes or a scalar.
On supported little-endian targets lane 0 occupies the low bits.
Zero-extend source carriers to total width, shift by cumulative widths and OR in source-lane order; extract by logical right shift and truncation in destination-lane order.
Omit identity casts and zero shifts; N22 legalises total widths above 128.
Drop no source memory access.
Every vector load/store follows the vector's datalayout bit string: lane k begins at bit k·bitwidth(T), with no scalar allocation padding between lanes.
`getelementptr T, ptr p, i64 k` followed by load/store T is permitted only when T's allocation stride equals that lane spacing.
Otherwise byte-sized lanes use `getelementptr i8, ptr p, i64 (k·bitwidth(T)/8)`; sub-byte lanes use packed-byte extraction/insertion.
Replacement accesses stay within the original vector storage range.
At byte offset o, scalar alignment is min(abi-align(T), gcd(original alignment,o)); gcd(a,0)=a.
Masked accesses touch only bytes containing active lanes and preserve inactive bits; padding follows N22.
This applies also to byte-multiple integer lanes such as i24, not only packed i1.
See [LangRef vector layout](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#vector-type) and [load/store semantics](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#load-instruction);
`insertelement`, `extractelement` with constant in-range indices and `shufflevector` with valid indices: lane renaming; N15 has already removed constant out-of-range extraction/insertion.
With a non-constant index (after N15): a `select` chain over the L lanes in lane order, using the same widened unsigned index and exact lane constants as N15.
Constants must never wrap to iK.
Insertion may fuse the out-of-range unchanged-vector select into per-lane equality selects: all equalities are false out of range.

LLVM admits an index of any integer width, independent of L ([extractelement](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#extractelement-instruction), [insertelement](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#insertelement-instruction)); LangRef out-of-range poison is totalised by N15, not by truncating L;

`llvm.vector.reduce.<op>(v)` with op ∈ {add, mul, and, or, xor, smax, smin, umax, umin, fadd, fmul, fmax, fmin, fmaximum, fminimum}: a **left fold** in lane order: `%nz.f1.r = <op> lane0, lane1`, `%nz.f<k>.r = <op> %nz.f<k−1>.r, lane k`, the last named `%r`; the ordered `fadd`/`fmul` forms take the start value as the first operand.
Exact for floating point once N2 has removed `reassoc`;
Selector/reduction exceptions take precedence over the next bullet.
For `vp.select` and `vp.merge`, the condition selects true/false operands within evl; false is not inactivity.
Outside evl, merge preserves on_false, select's poison becomes N7 zero.
VP reductions fold the start with active lanes only in increasing lane order; inactive lanes contribute no zero (unless zero is the reduction identity).

`llvm.vp.*` (vector-predicated) and `llvm.masked.*`: lane k is active iff k < evl and mask[k]; an active lane executes the scalar operation, an inactive lane yields the passthrough operand (masked loads) or 0 (N7: LangRef's poison), and a masked or predicated store, scatter or compress-store writes only active lanes, each under a conditional branch (blocks `nz.ml<k>.<r>`); gathers and scatters use the lane's pointer;

`llvm.stepvector` lane k is k; `llvm.get.active.lane.mask(base, n)` lane k is base + k < n (unsigned); `llvm.experimental.get.vector.length(cnt, vf, scalable)` is umin(cnt, vf·(V if scalable else 1)); `cttz.elts` is the index of the first nonzero lane (L if none, or the poison-free 0 of N7 when the flag says zero is poison); `loop.dependence.raw/war.mask(a, b, size)` lane k follows LangRef's definition;

`vector.extract`, `vector.insert`, `vector.reverse`, `vector.splice*`, `vector.interleave<n>`, `vector.deinterleave<n>`, `experimental.vector.compress`, `experimental.vector.histogram.*`, `experimental.vector.match`, `experimental.vector.extract.last.active`, `vector.partial.reduce.*`: lane permutations and folds by their LangRef definitions;

a vector parameter or result of an internal device function becomes L scalar parameters or an aggregate of L scalars in lane order; a vector that crosses an external boundary (a device entry's signature, a call of a function without a definition) is rebuilt with `insertelement` at that boundary, which only H code and the native build see.

Let w_k = min(64, N − 64k).
Limbs a_k, b_k (k = 0 … L − 1) have type i<w_k>.
Every limb operation, constant and incoming carry uses w_k, with an identity conversion when widths agree (in particular an i1 carry into an i1 top limb needs no zext):

`add`: `%nz.m0.r = add a_0, b_0`, `%nz.c0.r = icmp ult %nz.m0.r, a_0`; for k ≥ 1: `%nz.t<k>.r = add a_k, b_k`, `%nz.z<k>.r = zext i1 %nz.c<k−1>.r to i<w_k>`, `%nz.m<k>.r = add %nz.t<k>.r, %nz.z<k>.r` and, for k < L − 1, `%nz.u<k>.r = icmp ult %nz.t<k>.r, a_k`, `%nz.v<k>.r = icmp ult %nz.m<k>.r, %nz.t<k>.r`, `%nz.c<k>.r = or i1 %nz.u<k>.r, %nz.v<k>.r`;
`sub`: let beta_-1=0.
At limb k compute t_k=a_k−b_k modulo 2^w_k, z_k=zero-extended beta_(k−1) (identity if w_k=1), and m_k=t_k−z_k modulo 2^w_k.
When another limb follows, beta_k=(icmp ult a_k,b_k) OR (icmp ult t_k,z_k).
Discard the final outgoing borrow.
Canonical names use `%nz.m0.r = sub a_0,b_0`, `%nz.c0.r = icmp ult a_0,b_0`; thereafter `%nz.t<k>.r`, `%nz.z<k>.r`, `%nz.m<k>.r`, `%nz.u<k>.r`, `%nz.v<k>.r`, `%nz.c<k>.r` in that order.
In particular v_k tests t_k<z_k, never m_k<t_k.

This derives wrapping subtraction from [LangRef sub](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#sub-instruction) and [usub.with.overflow](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#llvm-usub-with-overflow-intrinsics);

`and`, `or`, `xor`: per limb; `icmp`: lexicographic from the top limb (signed on the top limb only for signed predicates); `select`, `phi`: per limb; `zext`, `sext`, `trunc`: limb copies; `sext` extracts the sign at bit w_top − 1, sign-extends the old partial top limb when widening it, and fills each new limb with that sign at its own width;

`mul`, `udiv`, `sdiv`, `urem`, `srem`, `shl`, `lshr`, `ashr`: calls of the runtimes entry points `__bennett_rt_i<N>_<op>(ptr r, ptr a, ptr b)` on shadow-stack slots holding the limbs (division by zero calls `__bennett_nz_fault(5)`, signed MIN / −1 `__bennett_nz_fault(6)`, shifts by ≥ N give 0 as N14);
loads and stores: per limb at offsets 8k, little-endian targets (`%nz.p<k>.r` / `%nz.q<k>.r` for the addresses);
a wide parameter or result of an internal device function becomes L limb parameters or an aggregate of limbs.

At W>128, the arithmetic expansions below (smax/smin/umax/umin, abs, scmp/ucmp, .with.overflow and .sat families) are emitted at width W and legalised by the repeated N22 (§12.1): carries/borrows, lexicographic compares, and per-limb select.
Aggregate expansion results carry the limb tuple plus the flag; insertvalue/extractvalue transport these fields without a residual wide aggregate.
Unsigned add overflow is the outgoing carry of the top limb; unsigned sub overflow is its outgoing borrow (retain it for the flag even though ordinary wrapping add/sub discards it).
Signed overflow tests signs at the true top bit.

Runtime rows bswap, bitreverse, ctpop, ctlz, cttz, fshl, fshr, sshl.sat, ushl.sat, smul/umul.fix[.sat], sdiv/udiv.fix[.sat], pdep, pext and clmul use `void @__bennett_rt_i<W>_<name>(ptr dst, ptr a[, ptr b, ptr c][, scalar flags])` instead of a wide call result/parameter.
Each wide argument is a limb slot; scalar flags retain their declared types, in source order.
Counts ctpop/ctlz/cttz write a full W-bit result slot.
Slots use §13.1's push/store/call/load/pop order (destination first, then wide source operands in order); runtime fault rows are unchanged.
These are the same limb-slot conventions as wide mul/div in §12.7.

`abs(a, false)` | `%nz.c.r = icmp slt a, 0`; `%nz.n.r = sub 0, a`; `%r = select i1 %nz.c.r, %nz.n.r, a`

**Wide conversion and intrinsic witnesses.** Limb [0,0,1] is 2^128, whose binary64 exponent is 1151 and fraction zero: carrier 0x47f0000000000000.
The source conversion probes are folded with LLVM before native code generation (the x86 backend lacks direct i192 conversion libcalls); the materialised limb output executes dynamically.
Both paths run with clang 18/23.
Truncating −2.5 toward zero gives −2 (all upper limbs ones); positive 1e300 saturates to 2^191−1.
In addition, [all-ones,0,0]+[1,0,0] carries into limb 1 but not beyond limb 2, whereas all-ones×3 plus one wraps to zero with overflow 1.
Population count of [all-ones,1,0] is 64+1=65.

The scalar GEP fast path of §12.6 exempts only lanes whose scalar allocation stride equals their vector bit spacing; n-vector-i24 above checks the padded-byte case.
For byte 0x80, bit 7 = 1; 2^128−1 carries through two 64-bit limbs into the one-bit limb; −1 sign-fills.

The validator (§12.4) on a residue and on clean code:
NS §3.2: "Floating point is deterministic soft-float in both builds … Hardware floating point never executes in either build."
Every floating-point construct of every format has a row here; none faults.
**Formats and carriers:**
`bfloat` | `bf16` | `i16`
`double` | `f64` | `i64`

The rewrite of an instruction `%r` with floating-point operands or result is: first, for each floating-point operand k (value or constant, in operand order), `%nz.<k>.r = bitcast <T> <operand> to <carrier>`; then the call below, named `%nz.i.r`; then, for a floating-point result, `%r = bitcast <carrier> %nz.i.r to <T>`.
The entry points are defined by `bennett-arith` and are part of its bitcode the driver links.
B below is the format's suffix, C its carrier.
`fadd`, `fsub`, `fmul`, `fdiv`, `frem` | `C @__bennett_sf_{add,sub,mul,div,rem}_B(C, C)` | bitcast

`fcmp

` | `i1 @__bennett_sf_cmp_B(C, C, i32 P)`, P the LLVM predicate number: `false` 0, `oeq` 1, `ogt` 2, `oge` 3, `olt` 4, `ole` 5, `one` 6, `ord` 7, `uno` 8, `ueq` 9, `ugt` 10, `uge` 11, `ult` 12, `ule` 13, `une` 14, `true` 15 | `%r` is the call itself

`sitofp`/`uitofp` from iM | `%nz.x.r = sext`/`zext iM a to i128` (omitted when M = 128), `C @__bennett_sf_{sitofp,uitofp}_B(i128)` | bitcast

**Wide integer sides (M>128).** The preceding i128 conversion rows apply only to M≤128.
For fptosi/fptoui, their .sat forms and lround/llround/lrint/llrint, N32 emits `void @__bennett_sf_<op>_B_wide(ptr d, C operand, i32 M)`.
Here d is a shadow-stack slot of L=ceil(M/64) limbs at byte offsets 8k (§12.7).
The entry writes the exact M-bit saturated result, limb 0 least significant, using truncation toward zero / the rounding rule above, with NaN mapped to 0; N22 loads each limb at width min(64,M−64k).
For sitofp/uitofp from iM, store all limbs in slot s and call `C @__bennett_sf_<op>_B_wide(ptr s, i32 M)`, correctly rounded from the exact signed/unsigned M-bit integer.
No i128 carrier intervenes.

For canonical temporary slots, emit ss_push(8L,8), then limb GEP/store rows in increasing k; for destinations, push then call then limb GEP/load rows in increasing k; pop slots in reverse push order after their last use.
Bitcast FP operands before destination push and FP results after pop.
The usual shadow-stack checks, budget charges and linked-runtime materialisation apply.
The helper's suffix op is fptosi/fptoui for the corresponding .sat form.

**Semantics of the entry points** (the contract with `bennett-arith`): IEEE 754-2019 for binary16 (`half`), binary32, binary64 and binary128; `bfloat` is the IEEE-style format with 8 exponent and 7 fraction bits; `x86_fp80` is the 80-bit x87 extended format (64-bit significand with explicit integer bit; encodings with exponent ≠ 0 and integer bit 0, the unnormals, and pseudo-denormals and pseudo-infinities are treated as NaN inputs, as modern x87 hardware does); `ppc_fp128` is double-double with the operations of LLVM's APFloat `PPCDoubleDouble` semantics of the major in use.

For all formats: round to nearest ties to even, subnormals supported, no observable flags or exceptions (except §13.5); **every NaN result is the format's canonical NaN** (sign 0, quiet bit set, other payload bits 0: `0x7E00` f16, `0x7FC0` bf16, `0x7FC00000` f32, `0x7FF8000000000000` f64, `0x7FFFC000000000000000` f80, `0x7FFF8000…0` f128, and for ppcf128 the f64 canonical NaN in the high double and +0 in the low); `rem` is C `fmod` (exact, the sign of the dividend); `cmp` is LLVM's `fcmp` for the predicate; `fptosi`/`fptoui` and the `.sat` forms truncate toward zero, map NaN to 0 and saturate values outside the range of iM to its bounds, returned sign-extended (`fptosi`) or zero-extended (`fptoui`) in i128 when M≤128, and in the full limb slot when M>128; `sitofp`/`uitofp` round to nearest even; `minnum`/`maxnum` are IEEE 754-2008 minNum/maxNum (one NaN operand: the other operand; two: the canonical NaN) with −0 < +0; `minimum`/`maximum` are IEEE 754-2019 (either NaN: the canonical NaN) with −0 < +0; `minimumnum`/`maximumnum` are IEEE 754-2019 minimumNumber/ maximumNumber; `sqrt`, `fma` and every rounding function are correctly rounded (`round` ties away from zero, `rint` and `nearbyint` to nearest even); `fpext` is exact; `fptrunc` rounds to nearest even; `canonicalize` maps every NaN to the canonical NaN and is the identity otherwise; `is.fpclass` tests LangRef's ten classes on the bit pattern; `ldexp`/`frexp` are exact up to rounding of a subnormal `ldexp` result; `lround`/`llround` round half away from zero and `lrint`/ `llrint` to nearest even, saturating like `fptosi`.

*(non-normative)* `fneg`, `fabs` and `copysign` stay bit-exact, so a NaN's sign bit set by `fneg` survives, as LangRef requires; an implementation of `half` and `bfloat` + − × ÷ √ in binary32 followed by one rounding is correctly rounded, since 24 ≥ 2p + 2 for p = 11 and p = 8 (Figueroa's double-rounding bound), but the contract is correct rounding, so `fma` needs its own implementation.
After N21 every vector floating-point operation is scalar: §13.1 applies lane by lane, and `vector.reduce.fadd`/`fmul` are the ordered left folds of §12.6 (exact once N2 has removed `reassoc`).

All seven formats of §13.1 are covered by the same table and contract (NS §3.2: "coverage-report lines until the library covers them"; `bennett-arith` covers them, so they are `lowered`). musl's `fmt_fp` (`printf("%Lf")`, rung 3) uses `x86_fp80` on x86-64 and `fp128` on AArch64 and RISC-V64.

`llvm.sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `exp`, `exp2`, `exp10`, `log`, `log2`, `log10`, `pow`, `powi`, `sincos`, `sincospi` and `modf` become calls of the **runtimes libm**: `@<name>` for `double`, `@<name>f` for `float`, and `@<name>l` for the target's native `long double` format D (x86-64: `x86_fp80`; AArch64 and RISC-V64: `fp128`).

For every other source format B, including half, bfloat and non-native x86_fp80/fp128/ppc_fp128, use a direct own-format carrier call `C_B @__bennett_sf_<name>_<suffix>(C_B, …)`; C_B and suffix are exactly §13.1's table.
No conversion through D is emitted.
All seven source formats remain covered on every supported platform; a format different from D is neither rejected nor trapped.
This route preserves the source format's precision and cannot request a narrowing fpext or an equal-size cross-format cast.
For these carrier calls, bitcast each floating operand k to its **own** carrier in operand order as `%nz.<k>.r`, call as `%nz.i.r`, and bitcast the scalar floating result back as `%r` (§13.1).
Retain non-floating operands and their types in source order.

These linked bennett-arith/runtimes functions implement the named operation numerically in B, using the same deterministic, versioned implementation in both builds; they are not bit reinterpretations between FP formats and do not use the host C long-double ABI.
NaN results use §13.1's canonical encoding, with signed zeros preserved where the operation requires.
As for the native-format libm below, no correct-rounding claim is made.

`powi(x,n)` retains repeated-squaring semantics (compiler-rt's `__powidf2`), with the integer exponent unconverted; its carrier spelling is `C_B @__bennett_sf_powi_<suffix>_i<K>(C_B, iK)` at the intrinsic's exponent width K (the floating-ABI spelling remains `__bennett_rt_powi_B`).
`sincos(x)` is the pair (sin x, cos x), `sincospi(x)` the pair (sinpi x, cospi x), and `modf(x)` the pair (fractional, integral).

Direct calls lower to CC/R `call` (ISA §4.1) and to lifted `lift.call`/`lift.ret` lprocs (ISA §3.7), with the depth and stack faults of the budget (§9).
Recursion is unrestricted.

**Candidate set** of an indirect call with callee value v: every `FN(F)` atom of AV(v) (§5), resolved through aliases; if AV(v) has the ⊤ flag, in addition every function whose LLVM function type equals the call's and whose address is used anywhere in the linked program (sound for defined C, C++ and Rust: a call through an incompatible type is undefined, and compatible C types lower to the same LLVM type under opaque pointers; SQLite §3).
The device closure includes every candidate (§4.1).

**Dispatch**: the compare tree of §16.4 over the candidates' A(F) values, sorted unsigned, with a static call at each leaf: CC/R `icmp eq` + `br` + `call @F_k` (ISA §4.1), lifted `lift.icmp.eq` + `qbranch` + `lift.call @L(F_k)` (ISA §4.2).
`qjumpr` is intra-function only (ISA §4.2) and is not used for calls.

**No match** (a value that is the address of no function of the program, or of a function without bitcode): F(4) `FAULT_UB_TRAP` (outline E13; calling through such a pointer is undefined or reaches code without bitcode, which the coverage report names).
**Zero candidates**: F(4) at the site.

**Trampolines** (`llvm.init.trampoline(t, f, nval)`, `llvm.adjust.trampoline(t)`): `init` stores the tag `0x42454E54` (i32), A(f) and nval in the trampoline memory t (runtimes `__bennett_rt_tramp_init`); `adjust` returns t.
Before the compare tree, an indirect call whose callee value v points to a live allocation holding the tag at offset 0 calls the stored function with the stored nest value as its `nest` argument.
Calls through a variadic function type use §14.3.
The same compare-tree construction serves region operands (§7.2), handle ids (§6.5), descriptor shapes (§8.4), `switch` (§14.8) and `indirectbr` (§14.9).

A variadic definition `R @f(P…, ...)` becomes `R @f(P…, ptr %nz.va)`; every call of it, direct or through a variadic function type, passes a **va block** in place of the variadic arguments.

A call site spills its variadic arguments (as the front end promoted them) into a va block `%nz.vb.<r>`, an alloca of the caller's entry block (so N24 places it in the caller's shadow frame), in argument order: argument j at the next offset aligned to max(8, ABI alignment of its type), occupying its size rounded up to 8 bytes (the x86-64 System V, AAPCS64 and RISC-V LP64 memory-argument layout); argument j ≥ 1 is addressed by `%nz.vb<j>.<r>`.
`llvm.va_start(ptr ap)` builds the target's `va_list` so that the front end's inline `va_arg` takes its memory path:

x86-64 System V | `{ i32 gp_offset, i32 fp_offset, ptr overflow_arg_area, ptr reg_save_area }` | gp_offset = 48, fp_offset = 176, overflow_arg_area = `%nz.va`, reg_save_area = null (SQLite §5.1): every `va_arg` finds no register slot left
AArch64 AAPCS64 | `{ ptr __stack, ptr __gr_top, ptr __vr_top, i32 __gr_offs, i32 __vr_offs }` | __stack = `%nz.va`, __gr_top = __vr_top = null, __gr_offs = __vr_offs = 0
RISC-V LP64 | `ptr` | the pointer `%nz.va`

The stores are named `%nz.vfo.<r>` (x86-64 `fp_offset` address), `%nz.vov.<r>` (overflow area address), `%nz.vrs.<r>` (register save area address); AArch64 and RISC-V use `%nz.vs.<r>`, `%nz.vgt.<r>`, `%nz.vvt.<r>`, `%nz.vgo.<r>`, `%nz.vvo.<r>` in field order.
IR `va_arg` is expanded by the same memory layout; `llvm.va_copy(d, s)` copies the `va_list` record (24, 32 or 8 bytes); `llvm.va_end` is deleted.
A call of an external variadic function without bitcode passes the va block to its host call (§11.4) or is trapped (§4.5).

The runtimes keep the **EH state** in the global `__bennett_rt_eh` of type `{ i32 active, i32 selector, ptr object }` (active: 0 none, 1 exception, 2 longjmp, 3 fiber switch, 4 exit; §14.5– §14.7).
Every device variant is rewritten, and the native comparison build uses the same materialised code, so the behaviour is identical in both builds:
`invoke F(args) to label %N unwind label %U` → `call F(args)`; `%nz.ehl.<r> = load i32, ptr @__bennett_rt_eh`; `%nz.ehc.<r> = icmp ne i32 %nz.ehl.<r>, 0`; `br i1 %nz.ehc.<r>, label %U, label %N`.

A `call` of a function that may unwind (one without `nounwind`, or an indirect call) inside a function that may unwind → the same check after the call, branching on a set flag to the function's **early-return block** `nz.ehr.<f>`, which pops the shadow frame (§17.3) and returns the zero of the return type.

`%r = landingpad T clauses` → `%r = call { ptr, i32 } @__bennett_rt_eh_match(ptr P, ptr @nz.lp.<f>.<r>)`, where P is the function's personality and `@nz.lp.<f>.<r>` is the private constant `{ i64 cleanup, i64 n, [n x { i64 kind, ptr info }] }` of the clauses in order (kind 0 `catch` with its typeinfo, kind 1 `filter` with its array).

The runtimes implement the personality's matching: for `__gxx_personality_v0`, C++ catch by typeinfo with the C++ ABI's derived-class rules and filters; for `rust_eh_personality`, Rust panics; for `__gcc_personality_v0`, cleanups only.

A matching catch or a cleanup clears `active` and returns (object, selector) with selector = `llvm.eh.typeid.for` of the matched typeinfo (0 for a cleanup); when nothing matches (or the pseudo-exception is a longjmp, switch or exit, which no clause handles) the flag stays set, the selector is −1, and the normaliser's check after the call (`%nz.ehm.<r> = extractvalue … 1`, `icmp eq … −1`) branches to the early-return block.
`resume v` → `call void @__bennett_rt_eh_resume({ ptr, i32 } v)` (sets `active` = 1 and the object) and a branch to the early-return block.
`llvm.eh.typeid.for(ti)` → `call i32 @__bennett_rt_eh_typeid(ptr ti)`; `llvm.eh.exceptionpointer` and `llvm.eh.exceptioncode` read the state's object.

`__cxa_throw`, `_Unwind_RaiseException`, `_Unwind_Resume`, `__rust_start_panic` are runtimes functions that set the state and return; the code after their call is the check above, and the original `unreachable` after them is kept on the path where the flag is clear (F(4)).
Windows funclet pads (`catchswitch`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, `catchret`, `cleanupret`) use the same transform with the `__CxxFrameHandler3` matching rules (corpus case needed, bd `-kdj`).

**Unwinding out of a region**: a set flag when an oracle's region function returns is `fault 4` in the wrapper (§16.2); in an action's generation it is TDL-12's `fault` event with code 4; at an R entry or a CC device entry it ends the run with code 4 (§11.5).

**Switch primitives**: the runtimes' `swapcontext`, `makecontext`, `setcontext`, Julia's task switch (`jl_swap_fiber`, `ctx_switch`), and the platform shims `swtch` and `__switch_to` (§20.5); all are implemented by `__bennett_rt_fiber_switch(from, to)` over records that hold a fiber's shadow stack (the `makecontext` stack argument) and its saved frame chain.

Every function on a call-graph path to a switch primitive is **instrumented**, Asyncify-style: its SSA values that are live across a call that may switch are spilled to its shadow frame before the call and reloaded after it, and it gets a resume index (the call site it was suspended at).

A switch sets the EH state to `active` = 3 and propagates (§14.4): each instrumented frame on the way out saves its resume index and returns early, up to the fiber's base; the runtime records the chain, then **rewinds** the target fiber: it calls the target's base with the rewind state, and each instrumented frame jumps to its saved resume index, reloads its values and calls the next frame, until the target's switch call returns.
This works in CC, R and L on ISA 0.8: it is ordinary code over memory.

The lifting map turns a materialised region function, a binding shape (§8.4) and the link layout (§19.5) into the **reference object** of that shape: the ISA object whose oracle `@ref` defines F_B and the budget unit by the reference interpreter (ISA §4.2 "Reference body and binding", §14.1).
It is a function of its inputs alone, so two plugins on the same LLVM version and pipeline produce byte-identical reference objects.
Its version (`map 0.2.9`) is the certificate's `dialect_mapping_version` (ISA §12.3).
The plugin's device objects (§17.4) are plugin-defined; they MUST be extensionally equal to the reference objects (ISA §5.7, T6; §18.7).
Every materialised function is liftable (outline B1): §12 legalises every construct into integer SSA values of at most 128 bits, memory, calls and branches at the map boundary.
Materialised LLVM may still contain bit-exact FP forms and aggregates; §16.4 maps these through integer carriers and field locations.
Every such accepted form has a row.
0.1's `BD-E-LIFT-SUBSET` is deleted.
For a shape with region function f, the reference object is the ISA text (ISA §16) with:
the header `bennett-object isa=0.8 object=0.8 launch=0.8 sched=0.8 cert=0.8 coverage=0.8 target=0.8 ptr_width=<pw>`;

`section symbols`: one JCS line, keys `"0"`, `"1"`, … in the order `@ref`, `@L1` … `@Ln`, then the data symbols `G…` in `section data` order, each with its kind, name, signature (ISA §9.1; `args` types spelled as JCS strings of the ISA §16.2 type, e.g. `"i64"`) and interface hash (ISA §9.2);

`section functions`: `@ref`, then the lprocs `@L1` … `@Ln`: one per function of the L closure of f (direct calls and indirect-call candidates), numbered in depth-first preorder from `@ref` along the `lift.call` rows in text order;

`section data`: one line `G<n> <hex>` per global of the layout below, in `layout.globals` key order, with the global's initialiser bytes after §12 (function addresses encoded as A(F) in P(a)-bit little-endian at each pointer field, §4.4; pointers to globals as their bases plus offsets);
`section layout`: one JCS line (§16.3).
**The wrapper `@ref`.** Its header is `oracle @ref (<ins>) (tgt:wire[T]) (fault:wire[4]) (<mems>) (<args>)`:
`<ins>`: `x<k>:wire[n] in` for the k-th `IN` binding in parameter order (n = n(q));
T: the width of the variant's slice (§8.6), or 1 when the shape has no output;

`<mems>`: first `coh:region[A,8] in` when a slice or oracle reads an arena object, then `m<k>:region[A,8] in` for the k-th `MEM_IN` binding in parameter order, then `e0` for an ENTROPY binding, `k0` for a BLOCK binding, `s0` for an entry-state snapshot (§8.5);
`<args>`: `a<k>:i<W>` for the k-th `ARG` binding in parameter order (W = P(a) for a `ptr addrspace(a)`).
Its body is one block `^entry():` with, in order:

**Prologue** (each part only when needed): the entry-state replay `t = lift.call @L(__bennett_rt_entry_replay) (s)` with `s = lift.addr @s0`; the device-state stores of §11.3 (for ENTROPY: `d0 = lift.addr @e0`, `d1 = lift.addr @G(base)`, `lift.boundscheck d1 8`, `lift.store.i64 d1 d0`, `d2 = lift.const.i64 <2^A>`, `d3 = lift.addr @G(size)`, `lift.boundscheck d3 8`, `lift.store.i64 d3 d2`; the position starts at its data image 0; the other models likewise in model order); the shadow-stack setup `t = lift.call @L(__bennett_rt_ss_init) (c)` with c = `lift.const.i64 <sstack>` (baseline for the provisional object, resolved for the final object under §9.2; no rematching) when the closure contains a call of `__bennett_rt_ss_push` (§17.3).

**Arguments**, for each parameter i in order: `IN` with n = W: the pseudo-location `x<k>` itself; `IN` with n < W: `w<i> = lift.zext.iW x<k>` (`lift.sext` for SEXT); `ARG`: `a<k>` itself; `MEM_IN`: `w<i> = lift.addr @m<k>`; `OUT`: `w<i> = lift.alloc <size>`.
**Call**: `r = lift.call @L1 (<arguments>)` (`r:reg[R]`, R the return width, 1 for `void`).

**Unwind check** (only when f may unwind, §14.4): `e = lift.addr @G(__bennett_rt_eh)`, `lift.boundscheck e 4`, `l = lift.load.i32 e`, `z = lift.const.i32 0`, `u = lift.icmp.ne l z`, `lift.faultif u 4`.

A function **may unwind** iff it is not `nounwind` and calls (directly or through a candidate) a function that may unwind, an external function without `nounwind`, or one of the raise functions of §14.4 (least fixpoint).

**Common delivery**, identical in every W_j: compute and validate *every* payload slice in output/slice order (§8.6), including all address offsets, bounds checks, loads, casts, dropped-bit checks and console slices.
Store each projection in `p<j>:reg[w_j]`.
Only after this identical sequence does `lift.retval p<j>` select this variant's result.
For k=0 there are no projections or dropped-return-bit checks: discard r and emit `p0 = lift.const.i1 0` followed by `lift.retval p0`, with `p0:reg[1]`.
These two terminal rows are part of the charged reference body, after the call and any unwind check.
A fault still delivers code through the four-wire fault interface and zero payload to the hidden bit.
For k=1 retain the original direct result without a projection move.
Every variant has the same location list and row charges, including unused projections.

The per-slice computation is: for the `tgt` output with n(tgt) < R: `c = lift.const.iR <n(tgt)>`, `t = lift.lshr r c`, `z = lift.const.iR 0`, `u = lift.icmp.ne t z`, `lift.faultif u 4` (the dropped-bits check of §8.2, in every variant); then the slice value: from `r` by `lift.lshr` of its low bit position (when nonzero) and `lift.trunc`/`lift.zext` to T (when the widths differ); from an `OUT` buffer `w<i>` by `p = lift.add w<i> <offset>` (when nonzero), `lift.boundscheck p <T/8>`, `v = lift.load.i<T> p`; then `p<j> = lift.mov <value>`; after all slices, `lift.retval p<selected>`.

Wrapper locations are `w<i>` (arguments), `r` (the call's result), `d<k>` (prologue), `p<j>` (delivery projections, including synthetic `p0` for k=0), and `c<j>`, `t<j>` for its constants and temporaries in emission order.

**lprocs.** Each lifted function g becomes `lproc @L<n> (a0:reg[W0], …) (r:reg[R]) () () ()` with the parameters in order (`ptr addrspace(a)` → `reg[P(a)]`; an aggregate parameter flattened into one parameter per field in field order), the result `r` of the return width (1 for `void`, whose `ret void` is `lift.ret r`), a `regs` line, and the blocks of §16.4.
The entry-state dependency decision of §8.5 precedes every private allocation in the wrapper prologue (§16.2), including device buffers and ss_init.
Replay allocates the caller's sizes in order, frees dead entries, and preserves bump/liveness even when no caller byte is read.
No fresh allocator reset is permitted for an allocation-only closure.
the i-th parameter of g | `a<i>` (fields of a flattened aggregate `a<i>_<f>`)
the k-th instruction of g that produces a value (0-based, in layout order, phis included) | location `v<k>` (fields of an aggregate value `v<k>_<f>`)
the j-th constant materialisation of g, in text order of the output | location `c<j>`
the j-th mapping temporary of g, in text order | location `t<j>`
the i-th basic block of g (0-based, layout order) | block `^b<i>`
a block created by a compare tree in block i (§16.4), in creation order | `^b<i>.s<j>` (j ≥ 1)
for the q-th indirect call of block i (q ≥ 1): the leaf of candidate k (sorted order), the default, the continuation | `^b<i>.q<q>c<k>`, `^b<i>.q<q>d`, `^b<i>.q<q>r`
the edge block from block i to block s | `^b<i>.e<s>`
the n-th global of the layout (1-based, in link order) | data symbol and global `G<n>`

The `regs` line lists every location of the function that is neither a parameter nor the result, in order of first appearance as a destination in the text, as `name:reg[W]`, separated by `, `; it is omitted when empty.

**Layout.** The reference object's `layout` is the device link layout (§19.5) restricted to the non-arena globals that the L closure names in `lift.addr` and, transitively, non-arena globals their initialisers point to (in link order, numbered G1, G2, …), with the link's `ptr_width`, `null_size`, `heap_base`, `heap_limit_max`, `H`, `A_tab` and `S_cells`, and `interface_regions` = { "ref": the shape's regions }.
An arena-relocated global has no G<n> symbol or data image: its address is @coh plus its arena offset.
`coh` is placed at A_coh (§19.5), disjoint from globals and heap.

Bases of all other regions follow `<mems>` order: each base is the smallest multiple of the region's size that is ≥ the end of the previous range (the heap's end `heap_base + heap_limit_max` for the first when there is no arena; otherwise the arena's end).

H is the smallest value with every range inside [0, 2^H); A_tab is the smallest value with 2^A_tab ≥ P + `heap_limit_max`, P the link's number of globals plus the largest number of interface regions of any oracle, so that allocation-table overflow never precedes heap exhaustion (both fault with code 2, ISA §4.2, and a reference object with fewer pre-entries than the device object faults at the same allocation); S_cells is the smallest value with 2^S_cells ≥ the frozen `stack` capacity of §9.2.
These link capacities are frozen before provisional identity construction and include unmatched raw entries and static non-sentinel record fields; identity overlays never recompute them.

Materialise null at P(a).

Physical boundscheck/load/store rows remain required; they do not substitute for the logical check.

The shape of the SQLite oracle of SQLite §5.2(i), route A, at toy size: a page image in a `MEM_IN` region (the database "fixed classically before entry", loaded into the register by `__bennett_qprep`), its classical length as an `ARG`, a superposed record key as a 3-wire `IN` (zero-extended to `i32`, like the 20-wire rowid), and a 1-wire target that receives an `i8` result through the dropped-bits check.
The library code is ordinary C with a recursive binary search, a function-pointer callback through a constant table (an indirect call with two candidates) and an error path that traps.
The image is: byte 0 the predicate id, byte 1 the record count n, then n records (key, value) sorted by key.

The quantum programmer's translation unit (outline §19.3: the normative route is a separate TU naming the unmodified function) applies one Grover iteration; it is linked with the library by `clang -O2 -flto` and the driver's `lto<O3>`, after which the module holds 4 `qalloc`, 2 `qprep`, 24 `gate`, 1 `gate3`, 1 `oracle`, 3 `measure` and 4 `qfree` calls (counted on LLVM 18):
*(non-normative)* The descriptor's kinds and the budget record's fields reach the marker as constant stores and `memset`s (PT7, PT8), so there is one shape.

The MEM_IN register is the static register of the root `db` (it is stored in the descriptor, so it has a static register file with N = 1 by §6.5 rule 1); `f` stays clean when the fault rate is zero, and `t` returns to |0⟩ after H and X.

There is one classical memory, shared by H, CC, R and the entry state of every L invocation (§8.5; NS §3.2):

**Live allocations**: a shadow-stack frame from its push to its pop (§17.3); a global, always; a heap allocation of the runtimes allocator from its allocation to its `free` (`free` of a null pointer does nothing).
The null region is never allocated.
**Zero fill**: shadow-stack frames and heap allocations are zero-filled in both builds; globals hold their initialisers.
Region inputs are not zero-filled: they are the bytes the host supplies (NS §3.2).

**Bounds**: a load, store or memory-function range is valid iff all its bytes lie in one live allocation (an address model: the object a pointer was derived from is irrelevant; NS §3.2 "faulting memory access is defined").

**Addresses**: the comparison link (§19.5) places globals and functions; the runtimes allocator's fixed base places the heap; the shadow stack is heap memory, so native stack addresses never reach device results.
The residue is host-stack addresses passed in by host code: executions in which they influence a result are *layout-dependent* (NS §3.2; §24 D12), validated against the reference interpreter.
**Single thread**: atomics and volatile are sequentialised (N9; NS §3.2; §24 D24).
The device `layout` (ISA §9.1) replicates the comparison link (§19.5).

statements.text: CC and R code use ISA §7.1 memory; L code uses ISA §7.2 memory with the same `heap_base` and global bases, so addresses are equal in every tier.
NS §3.2: "Region allocas are rewritten by the normaliser onto a shim-managed shadow stack in both builds where possible"; in device variants it is always possible.
The runtimes provide, with these contracts:

`void __bennett_rt_ss_init(i64 size)` | is idempotent: if stack state is already set (by entry replay in an oracle), allocates nothing and keeps base, size and stack pointer; otherwise allocates one heap block of `size` bytes (`sstack`, §9.2), by `__bennett_nz_alloc`; called by the oracle wrapper prologue (§16.2), the R entry stub and the CC entry stub when their closure uses the shadow stack

`ptr __bennett_rt_ss_push(i64 size, i64 align)` | pushes a frame of `size` bytes aligned to `align` and returns its base; the frame is zero-filled; overflow of the block is `__bennett_nz_fault(2)` (`FAULT_BUDGET_HEAP`)
`void __bennett_rt_ss_pop(ptr fp)` | pops the frame fp and every frame pushed after it
`ptr __bennett_rt_ss_alloca(i64 n, i64 align)` | a zero-filled dynamic allocation in the current frame, released by its pop
`ptr __bennett_rt_ss_save()`, `void __bennett_rt_ss_restore(ptr)` | `llvm.stacksave`/`llvm.stackrestore`
Shadow-stack backing storage is physical storage, not a program allocation.
Maintain logical frame base, extent and liveness, including dynamic allocations, extensions and saved restore points.
A program access requires its entire nonwrapping byte range inside one live logical frame/allocation under §17.1; otherwise fault 7 before any access or mutation.
Containment in the backing ISA allocation is insufficient.
Push registers a live frame; pop invalidates it and every younger frame; restore invalidates released ranges, truncating a surviving dynamic extent at the saved limit.
Separate dynamic allocations in a frame keep their individual extents; an access may not span distinct live frames/allocations or unused capacity.
The address model permits a reused address once a new live logical allocation contains the complete range.

The default validation is the ordinary materialised runtime helper __bennett_rt_ss_check(p,n,table): reject wrapping ranges, visit logical entries in creation order, OR the live-and-contained predicates, and fault 7 if false.
Its rows and metadata updates are charged in §16's reference object, and both builds implement the same checks and stack layout.
Proven containment may eliminate the helper.

Runtime bookkeeping, zero-fill and entry replay use an explicit internal path restricted to backing storage and metadata, never exposed to source program accesses; it is not a blanket exemption for ordinary calls into runtime-named functions.
Replay the logical metadata as well as backing bytes under §8.5.

N24 rewrites each function with allocas: `%nz.fp.<f> = call ptr @__bennett_rt_ss_push(i64 S, i64 A)` at entry, where the static allocas of the entry block are laid out in instruction order, each at the next offset aligned to its alignment, S is the total rounded up to A, the largest alignment.
The pushed frame base is aligned to A; its end (the next frame start before any additional alignment) is base + S.

Each static alloca becomes `getelementptr i8, ptr %nz.fp.<f>, i64 <offset>` with the alloca's name; every other alloca becomes `__bennett_rt_ss_alloca`; `call void @__bennett_rt_ss_pop(ptr %nz.fp.<f>)` precedes every `ret` (including the early returns of §14.4).

`llvm.frameaddress(0)`, `llvm.sponentry`, `llvm.addressofreturnaddress`, `llvm.swift.async.context.addr` and `llvm.eh.dwarf.cfa` give `%nz.fp.<f>`; `llvm.frameaddress(n > 0)` and `llvm.returnaddress` give null (LangRef: "zero if it cannot be identified"); `llvm.stackaddress` gives the current shadow-stack pointer; `llvm.localescape` records the escaped allocas' offsets in a per-function table that `llvm.localrecover` reads with the parent's frame address; `llvm.structured.alloca` is an alloca.
All pointer conversions, carriers, memory widths and address bridges use P(a) and the incoming target conversion exactly as in §16.4, in CC/R and the native build alike.
Every GEP, including constant expressions, uses §16.4's datalayout pointer-index width and preserves higher pointer bits.
CC/R express its truncations, scaled modular offsets and high/low recombination with ordinary ISA integer operations.

This follows [LangRef GEP semantics](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#getelementptr-instruction) and [datalayout pointer indices](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#data-layout), not full-width pointer addition when I<P(a); differing widths do not reject a layout.

It is never an `-O0` build: optimisation legally changes marker operands (spike F4), and the materialised optimised module is the one program both builds implement.

The reference semantics runs H functions natively and every device entry, region invocation and whole-program entry on the materialised module over a state Σ = (C, Q, H, G, K, T):

**C**, the classical state: LLVM's semantics of the materialised module (LangRef), with every remaining choice fixed by §12–§14 and the fault outcomes of §17.5; it includes the shadows of the arena (TDL-4).
In particular GEP uses the pointer-index width, as fixed in §16.4 and §17.4, also in constant expressions; pointer representations and conversions use P(a), not an implicit pw-bit move;
**Q**, the quantum state of the ISA formal model (ISA §14.2): a unit vector over the live wires in allocation order, including the arena's wires (TDL-4);
**H**, the handle table: for each handle, its wires, whether it is live, and the generation it was allocated in, if any;
**G**, a stack of **recorders**, one per active generation (§18.4);
**K**, the coherence states of the object instances (TDL-2);
**T**, the device-model states and the effect tape (§11).
Measurement and `observe` make the semantics a tree: every outcome sequence has its Born probability (ISA §14.2) and its own continuation.
A marker call or a TDL store produces **events**: ISA-level operations, each with a **control set** (a set of wires, initially empty).
The forms are:
`qalloc H n`, `qfree H`; the gates `x h s sdg t tdg cx cz swap ccx` (ISA §4.4) and `rx θ`, `ry θ`, `rz θ` on wires; `qload D M A`, `qstore M A V`, `qprep H bytes`;
`oracle R B (ins..) tgt fault (mem..) (args..)` and `wide R …` (§8.6), `inplace G G′ B X`;
the TDL events of §10: `slice O (args..) (ins..) (mem..) -> regs`, `xmask X+o m`, `xstore X+a m`, `perm P X+a (params..)`, `xchg X+a h`, `fault C` (TDL-12), `firstfault (f..) Φ`;
`qcopy S -> D`: allocate D clean then XOR S into it; `quncopy S D`: XOR S into D and release clean D; `qxor S T`: T XOR= S; `copy F -> G` means qalloc G then qxor F G (TDL-8);
`observe X+o len`, `measure` (outside generations), `effect dev.op` (R).
When no recorder is active, an event is **applied** to Σ at once; otherwise it is appended to the innermost recorder.
Applying an event with control set S applies it only on the basis states where every wire of S is 1 (ISA `ctl`, ISA §4.7, §5.3); `qalloc` and `qfree` are unconditional (ISA §3.5).
Arena writes with nonempty control set, Co address or Co value first materialise Cl objects and make Cl or M objects Co.

Otherwise apply events per form: `xmask` XORs its mask into shadow only for Cl (arena stays zero), both copies for M, arena only for Co; `xstore` does the same XOR at its selected address; `perm` applies its bijection to shadow only for Cl, both copies for M, arena only for Co.

`xchg` with a Co register first materialises and makes X Co; with a classical basis operand it exchanges with shadow for Cl, both copies consistently for M (returning one old value), arena only for Co.
Unconditional Cl-valued xmask/xstore/perm leave K unchanged.
Event application does not also reapply its speculative generation-view update.
Event-application writes invalidate observation coverage; permitted TDL-11 CC stores retain it as covering writes.

The plugin realises applied events as CC-level region calls in event order (ISA §4.7), whose temporaries are released by `qreg.free` with the dynamic cleanliness check of ISA §3.3; it MAY compile an event list into one ISA action when that action satisfies ISA §6.

**Adjoint** of an event list (ISA §5.3 adjoint table): reverse the list and replace each event: `x h cx cz swap ccx qload qstore qprep oracle wide slice xmask xstore xchg` are self-adjoint; `s` ↔ `sdg`; `t` ↔ `tdg`; `rx θ` ↦ `rx −θ` (and `ry`, `rz`); `qalloc` ↔ `qfree` of the same wires; `inplace G G′ B X` ↦ `inplace G′ G B X`; `perm P` ↦ the library inverse of P.
Control sets are unchanged.
Ordinary workspace qcopy and quncopy are mutual adjoints.
A deferred-measurement qcopy is a channel record and is never adjointed to quncopy.
In standalone adj(f), keep non-record events in reverse-list order.
Insert each fresh retained record immediately before its earliest reversed consumer, after every reversed event preceding that consumer.
A record without consumers stays at its reversed source position.
Records in the same insertion gap follow original source order, with record producers before dependent records.
Thus record placement is deterministic, including when noncommuting events change its source.

For local sources, hoist required unconditional inverse allocations before their copies and retain the sources through their last use; this lifetime extension does not commute a copy across an arbitrary quantum operation.
Optimisations MUST preserve this complete instrument and the §7.5(a) measurement boundary.
In compute(f,use), E_f's records survive E_u and adjoint(E_f), which reuses these wires without copying or uncopying them, and measurement is at the first §7.5(a) boundary after compute returns.
A Co-loop adjoint is the inverse of the complete clean-workspace transition, not forward evaluation of the guard on the adjoint-entry mutable data.
For conditions on preserved inputs, compute flags forward, apply body adjoints for i=N..1, then uncompute the flags with their exact computing slices.

For overwritten inputs in a standalone adj, use the bounded inverse required by TDL-5(b) to reconstruct the unique forward entry on copies, compute its trajectory, apply the inverse iterations, and clean that reconstruction against the restored entry.
No assumed earlier invocation supplies this entry.
When no unique inverse exists on the declared interface, the existing TDL-5(d) applies; changing adj into an entry-guard instrument is not an alternative inverse.

Out-of-place evaluation and compute retain the computation under TDL-5(c). compute's adjoint(E_f) reuses the actual forward flags/history and cleans them as each iteration state is restored, without a fresh trajectory.
Only genuine measurement records and actual fault outputs have their separate retained lifetimes.
qxor and firstfault are self-adjoint XORs.
`fault C` is an xmask of C on a fresh declared fault register, also self-adjoint.
Adjoint of `copy F -> G` is qxor F G then qfree G, not another allocation.

**Leak rule** (successful source generation only, excluding the declared fault/measurement outputs): (`T-LEAK`): for `ctrl` and `adj`, every register allocated during the generation is freed during it; for `compute`, every register allocated during gen(use) is freed during it, while a register allocated during gen(f) and not freed during it is freed by adjoint(E_f), in which its `qalloc` event becomes a `qfree` event, so gen(use) MUST NOT free it (`T-FOREIGN`).
Outside generations the check is at program end (§6.6): a register that is still live then, neither freed by device code or the host (`bennett_qreg_free`) nor consumed by a `measure`, is `T-LEAK`.

NS §4.2 requires "allocations inside released clean or borrowed and restored": `T-LEAK` and `T-CLEAN` are those checks.

A plugin and an executor (ISA §1.2) together conform iff, for every module the rules accept or block, every host input and every sequence of measurement and `observe` outcomes, outside the executions that reach a blocker point: the probability of that sequence, every classical value the host observes (return values of device entries, memory they write, console output), every fault code and every trap equal those of the reference semantics; and the quantum state at every measurement and at every device-entry return equals the reference state, exactly when the program uses permutation gates only, and otherwise within the error bound its certificate states (ISA §12.3).
A program that reaches `T-CLEAN` in the reference semantics is erroneous; an executor that cannot test cleanliness (hardware) need not reproduce that trap (ISA §17 item 14).

native-comparable success | the reference completes without fault and no layout-dependent value influences the result | the artefact's results equal native
reference fault | the reference faults (code ≠ 0) | the artefact reports the same code; native supplies no cause (it may trap, silently read adjacent memory or hang)

layout-dependent | the reference interpreter's address provenance shows a host-stack address, or a `blockaddress` value (§14.9), influencing the result | validated against the reference interpreter instead of native, counted separately
classifier-flagged undefined | an instrumented build (UBSan, ASan, MSan) flags the input (NS §3.2) | excluded from comparison, counted separately

*(non-normative)* The states are those of 0.1 §8.8.
Control: after h, one controlled flip gives (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 and the second cancels it.
Adjoint: h|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, s multiplies the |1⟩ amplitude by i and t by e^{iπ/4}, so before the adjoint it is i·e^{iπ/4}/√2 = e^{i3π/4}/√2 = (−1 + i)/2.
Compute: h, cx give (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2; s s = Z on the ancilla gives (|00⟩ − |11⟩)/√2; the uncomputing cx gives (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2 ⊗ |0⟩, and h maps it to |10⟩; x returns a to |0⟩ before release.
**TDL.** The following programs exercise every case of TDL-5, TDL-10 and TDL-11 on the globals `@cnt` and `@other`, which are in the may-Co set (TDL-2) and hence in the arena.
Each device entry ends by observing both globals, so that MC's state at every device entry is empty (MC3; a host may call the entries in any order).
`text tdl=` blocks give the partition of each region and the run's events with their control sets; a register written `-> r:w` is a fresh register of w wires allocated by that event.
`text state=` blocks list the handles in allocation order and then the arena bytes of `@cnt` (and `@other`) in hex, as `|q…; cnt other>`.
Temporary and retained registers (TDL-7, TDL-8) hold 0 in these fault-free runs and are omitted.
Every Co read is from the arena; every slice is an oracle bound to the arena region `coh`.

Front ends emit bitcode with their stock pre-link pipelines; no Bennett code runs before the final link (Enzyme PR #3211: "forgetting it is a loud failure"), except in the explicit closed-unit mode (§19.7).

The driver links all bitcode inputs (§19.8), links `bennett-runtimes` and `bennett-arith` bitcode of the link's major M, runs the post-link pipeline (`lto<O3>` by default, or any envelope pipeline of §21.1 the user selects), then runs the plugin on the whole program (NS §3.3).
With `opt`:

```
opt -load-pass-plugin=libbennett-plugin-<M>.so -passes='lto<O3>,bennett' -bennett-dialect=0.2.10 …
```
The plugin runs on one merged module (full LTO; §24 D23).
It registers one module pass, `bennett`, and MAY register a full-LTO last extension point for use from a linker plugin; it MUST do nothing in a pre-link phase.

**Bitcode sources** (NS §3.3): Rust `std` from the bitcode embedded in rlibs (`.llvmbc`) where present and readable by §19.8, else `-Zbuild-std`; the Julia runtime by the runtimes' shim bitcode; every remaining call without bitcode is a `trapped` coverage line (§4.5).
The whole program is the device program in tier R (NS §4.2: "entered through `__bennett_reversible` or a driver mode"; rungs 3, 5, 6):

a CC **launch stub** fetches the argv and envp bytes with `hostcall bennett.argv`, initialises the shadow stack (§17.3), calls the R entry `<sym>` with (argc, argv, envp), catches the exit pseudo-exception (§14.7) and returns the status;
effects are the ISA device models (§11.2): console, clock, entropy (the launch's entropy tape), block with `block_image` from `--bennett-disk=<file>`;
un-run is `bennett_reverse` (ISA §10): whole-run reversal restores the entry state; tape replay is deterministic from the tape and the entropy;
a `measure` reachable in the program is `BD-E-REVERSIBLE-MEASURE` (§7.5b).

A convenience: the driver synthesises the translation unit a quantum programmer would write (§16.7): a CC function that builds a descriptor binding `<sym>`'s parameters by `--bennett-bind=<param>:<kind>:<width>[:<value>]` (kind `in`, `arg`, `mem_in`, `out`), device bindings by `--bennett-dev=<model>:<width>[:<value>]`, and a payload: the return value, the exit status caught by the wrapper (§14.7), or the first L bytes of console output (`--bennett-payload=return|exit|console:<L>`), and applies the oracle once to registers it allocates, as a device entry the host calls with those registers.
The normative route is the separate translation unit with marker calls naming the unmodified function (rungs 4, 7, 8).

H functions stay native unless they share **pointer-rich** memory with device code: a pointer argument of a device-entry call, or a global accessed by both, whose pointee may contain pointers that device code reads (§5).
Such H functions are **promoted** to CC variants, transitively up to their roots (in the limit `main`, and then H is the system-call proxy only: `hostcall bennett.syscall`).
Results are equal by the materialised semantics; ISA-11 would let them stay native (an efficiency and placement item, §25.3; outline E11).

The driver links the materialised module natively (§17.7) with a linker script that fixes the addresses: non-PIE; identical-code folding and constant merging off; the null region [0, `null_size`) with `null_size` = 4096; the data sections (`.rodata`, `.data`, `.bss`, in that order) from `data_base` = 4096; the text from `text_base` = 0x400000, or, when the device ranges below (data, heap, arena, interface regions, computed first) end above 0x400000, from the first multiple of 0x200000 at or after their end, so that the native comparison binary maps its code disjointly from them; the defaults are options (`--bennett-layout-data-base`, `--bennett-layout-text-base`, §24).
The link map gives A(F) for every function and the base of every global.
The device `layout` (ISA §9.1) replicates it:
`globals`: every global of the link at its link address with its image;
`heap_base`: the first multiple of 4096 at or after the end of the data; `heap_limit_max`: the largest `heap` of the budget table (which covers the shadow stack, §9.2);

the arena (TDL-4) at the first multiple of its size 2^A at or after the heap's end, with 2^A the smallest power of two covering the may-Co globals and the coherent allocator's heap (its size from `--bennett-arena-heap`, default the largest `heap` of the table); the arena's shadow `__bennett_rt_shadow` is a global of the data sections;
interface regions per oracle above the arena (§16.3); H, A_tab and S_cells by §16.3;
the production host image is linked with the same addresses for every function and global whose address may cross the boundary (§4.4).
*(non-normative)* With data low and text high, H covers the data, heap and regions; function addresses are values only and never occupy device memory.

`--bennett-snapshot=<dump>` rewrites the initialisers of the mutable globals listed in the dump (and the platform RAM global, §20.1) to the dump's bytes before the plugin runs; the data images then carry the snapshot and R of §8.5 is empty for them (rung 7: "kernel state snapshot fixed classically after boot").
The dump is recorded by hash in the build record.

`-bennett-closed-unit` (the REPL fast path, NS §3.3: "a per-TU invocation remains available as a fast path for programs closed within one unit, with the same semantics"): the plugin runs on one module plus the runtimes and arith bitcode, after a **closedness check**: every device function's callees are defined in that set or are trapped exactly as in whole-program mode; no device function's address escapes the module; no function pointer enters through a device-entry parameter.
If the check passes, processing is identical to whole-program mode.
If it fails, the driver falls back to whole-program mode (it does not reject).
Objects are content-addressed (ISA §9.2) and linked at launch (ISA §9.3), so the REPL is incremental.
The driver reads every bitcode input with the newest major M of the envelope (bitcode is readable by newer majors), links with M and runs plugin M; runtimes and arith ship bitcode for each M.
Every input MUST have one target datalayout and triple (NS §3.2) (`BD-E-VERSION` otherwise: a tool-version mismatch, not a program property).
An input newer than M is `BD-E-VERSION`.
The tested (front end, major) pairs are published in the envelope; a corpus case links clang 18 bitcode with Julia's and rustc's majors (§21.2; bd `.16`).

**Identity.** `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` returns plugin name `bennett` and version string `dialect-0.2.10;isa-0.8`; the driver refuses a plugin whose string differs.
One plugin build per LLVM major (NS §3.2).

**Outputs** (in `-bennett-out`, file names plugin-defined, §24 D22): the materialised device variants as bitcode (§17.7); the host module with device entries replaced by launch stubs; the ISA objects (ISA §9, §16); the certificate (ISA §12) with `producer.materialisation = {llvm_version, pipeline, normaliser_version: "0.2.8"}` and `bindings.dialect_mapping_version = "0.2.9"`; the coverage report (ISA §13), whose `source` field is `dialect-0.2.10:<rule id>` (e.g. `dialect-0.2.10:N33`); the blocker reports (§25.1); and the **build record**, one JCS object with the build flags, the budget table (resolved, including each shape's selection_identity, final semantic identity, resolved components and frozen layout capacities under §9.2) and its SHA-256, the runtimes, arith and asm-table hashes, the snapshot hash, the layout options and the `cpuid` leaf table (§15.2).
Its SHA-256 is recorded as the build metadata of the certificate's `producer.version` (`<driver version>+build.<hex>`) until the ISA certificate has a field for it (§25.2).

**A missing plugin fails loud.** No production artefact defines a marker: `bennett-runtimes`, `bennett-arith` and the driver's link inputs define no `__bennett_*` marker symbol (test runtimes such as the trace runtime do, and are never linked into production).
A link in which the plugin did not run therefore leaves undefined references and fails at link time; the driver MUST NOT ignore unresolved symbols or supply weak marker definitions.

**Module flag.** A producer MAY add `!{i32 1, !"bennett.dialect", !"0.2.10"}` (behaviour Error, so an LTO link of modules of two dialect versions fails); the plugin MUST reject a module whose flag differs from its version (`BD-E-VERSION`):
NS §5: "The kernel compiles, boots on the VM in the reversible tier with its devices modelled, writes a serial console to the tape, and un-boots to the reset vector."
This section fixes the mechanisms (outline E4: riscv64 first); its row lists come from the platform spike of §20.7, a mechanics deferral (§24): the capability is not in question (audit O-06).
A virtual board, selected by `--bennett-platform=riscv64-bennett-virt`:
statements.uncertain: no RFC keyword, defined term, example marker or declarative verb

statements.text: RAM: one runtimes global `__bennett_rt_platform_ram` of the configured size (`--bennett-platform-ram`, default 128 MiB), which the profile's linker script places at the board's physical base 0x80000000 after the other data (the heap and the text follow it by §19.5), so kernel physical addresses are ordinary device addresses;
the CSR file (privilege mode, `satp`, `stvec`, `mtvec`, `sstatus`, `mstatus`, `sie`, `sip`, `scause`, `sepc`, `stval`, `sscratch`, `mscratch`, `time`, …) as the runtimes global `__bennett_rt_csr`;
devices: a UART 16550 (console), a CLINT and timer (clock), a PLIC, and a virtio-blk MMIO device (block), each a runtimes C model over the effect markers.

The privileged forms are `shimmed` rows of §15: `csrr`, `csrw`, `csrs`, `csrc` (and the immediate forms) → `__bennett_rt_csr_read(i32 csr)`, `_write(csr, v)`, `_set(csr, v)`, `_clear(csr, v)`; `sfence.vma` → `__bennett_rt_sfence_vma(va, asid)`; `wfi` → `__bennett_rt_wfi()` (advances the clock model to the next timer event); `ecall` in kernel mode → `__bennett_rt_sbi_call(…)` (the SBI of the board), in user mode → the trap path of §20.4; `mret`, `sret` → `__bennett_rt_trap_return (mode)`; `fence.i` and `fence` → deleted (lowered).
The exact asm strings and constraint strings are those the §20.7 spike inventories.

Under the platform profile, N9 first routes every volatile load and store, and every MMIO asm form, to `__bennett_rt_mmio_{load,store}_i<N>(addr[, v])`; these dispatch by address range to the device models' handlers (C code in runtimes that calls the effect markers), and otherwise access memory.
A non-volatile access to an MMIO window lies outside every live allocation and faults with code 7, as the reference semantics defines (§17.1).

Poll points at loop back edges and function entries (N35) call `__bennett_rt_poll()`, which checks the timer model (deterministic, driven by the clock model) and the PLIC's pending bits; on delivery it sets the CSRs (`scause`, `sepc`, `stval`, `sstatus`) and calls the trap vector `stvec` by A(F) dispatch (§14.2).

Interrupts are therefore taken at poll points only, a deterministic choice recorded in the certificate; NS §3.2's single-thread assumption covers the uniprocessor kernel (`CONFIG_SMP=n`, xv6 `CPUS=1`).

The assembly entry points (`swtch`, `trampoline`, `uservec`, `userret`, `kernelvec`, Linux `__switch_to`, `handle_exception`, `ret_from_exception`) are platform shims by symbol (§15.3), written in C over the fibers of §14.6: a kernel context switch is a fiber switch; a trap entry saves the user registers into the trap frame from the platform register file and calls the kernel's handler; a trap return restores them and resumes the user fiber.

N35 translates **all guest memory accesses** in translation-enabled effective privilege contexts through the modelled satp and Sv39 page tables/permissions, including supervisor kernel accesses and user accesses (and effective privilege selected by MPRV for data).
statements.uncertain: no RFC keyword, defined term, example marker or declarative verb

statements.text: Bare/physical accesses use physical addresses.
Runtime model helpers and page-table walks access physical backing storage directly, and are excluded from reinstrumentation.
LLVM guest pointers remain virtual values through GEP, ptrtoint and comparisons; translate only on memory access.
The layout records virtual data/code addresses and their physical backing.
A physical RAM address and every permitted virtual alias name the same backing byte.
Indirect dispatch and trap resumption preserve this mapping: A(F), stvec and sepc retain guest virtual code addresses, resolved through the code-address map after Sv39 validation.
Translation failures deliver the modelled guest page/access trap before memory mutation; they are not accidental accesses to an unallocated high host/device address.
Runtime helpers avoid a second translation.
These rules apply equally to CC/R and L variants.

User programs are built to bitcode and linked into the device program under the comparison layout (§19.5); their ELF images on the disk image are the same link, so entry and function addresses are A(F).

`exec` and `sret` to user mode dispatch the user entry by A(F); user loads and stores go through a **soft-MMU**: N35 instruments all guest functions in translation-enabled privilege contexts with an Sv39 walk over the modelled `satp`, including supervisor kernel accesses, with guest page faults delivered through §20.4.

```text state=sv39-kernel-alias at=2
RAM physical P=0x80000000 holds 0x12
supervisor satp=Sv39; valid writable kernel V=0xffffffe000000000 maps to P
store 0x34 through V; load P -> 0x34; load V -> 0x34; no code 7
reverse store -> both P and V read 0x12; page-table state restored
```

Until then those rows are this section's patterns (§24).

statements.text: Each state block specifies the requested driver operation on the accompanying input, not just a recogniser verdict.
Missing driver/platform adapters fail under P-2; parsing alone never satisfies these scenarios.
**`driver-oracle-synthesis` (§19.3).** The input is an unmodified integer program.
Binding x to eight input wires gives wrapping x+1: x=7 gives 8 and x=255 gives 0.
The driver-generated descriptor has one IN, an eight-wire target and a four-wire fault; it launches one oracle invocation.
This is the synthesis obligation, not an assertion that parsing f executes the driver.

```text state=driver-oracle-synthesis at=0
driver: --bennett-oracle=program --bennett-bind=0:in:8 --bennett-payload=return
synthesise: nparam=1 IN(8,zext); tgt width=8; fault width=4; one invocation
input=7 -> code=0 payload=8
input=255 -> code=0 payload=0
```
**`driver-pointer-promotion` (§19.4).** The host mutation changes tail.value from 1 to 9.
statements.uncertain: no RFC keyword, defined term, example marker or declarative verb

statements.text: Device code follows head.next and reads 9.
Since head contains a pointer the device follows, the shared memory is pointer-rich: mutate and its root main must be promoted to CC.
Keeping a native host-only tail store without coherent state would instead leave the image value 1.

```text state=driver-pointer-promotion at=0
placement: mutate=CC main=CC device=CC; host retains only system-call proxy
run: main returns 9; device follows head.next; tail image 1 is not the call-entry value
```
**`driver-comparison-layout` (§19.5).** The first global occupies [4096,4099), the aligned pointer slot [4104,4112), so heap_base=8192.
statements.uncertain: no RFC keyword, defined term, example marker or declarative verb

statements.text: With heap_limit_max=4194304 the heap ends at 4202496, above 0x400000.
With no arena or interfaces, text begins at the next multiple of 0x200000: 6291456 (0x600000).
The initial pointer slot contains 4096 in little-endian; native and device layouts must agree.

```text state=driver-comparison-layout at=0
driver: data_base=4096 heap_limit_max=4194304; no arena/interface
layout: bytes=4096 slot=4104 heap_base=8192 heap_end=4202496 text_base=6291456
slot image=0010000000000000
native and device: f returns 7; no code/data overlap
```
**`driver-snapshot-initializer` (§19.6).** The dump supplies the single mutable byte g=7 before materialisation.
Its former zero image is replaced by 07; no function outside the closure writes g, so this build-time case needs no call-entry transfer.
Both builds return 7 from the same fixed image.

```text state=driver-snapshot-initializer at=0
driver: --bennett-snapshot=dump; dump bytes for @g=07
materialised global: @g = internal global i8 7
data image=07; entry read-set requiring transfer=empty; no snapshot register
native and device: f returns 7; build record includes dump SHA-256
```
**`driver-closed-unit-fallback` (§19.7).** The entry receives a function pointer, violating the closedness check even though g is defined and address-taken.
The requested fast path therefore falls back to the whole-program route; it does not reject the program.
Dispatching p=g returns 7 on either route.

```text state=driver-closed-unit-fallback at=0
driver: -bennett-closed-unit; entry parameter p supplies function pointer
closedness=false; selected route=whole-program; verdict=accept
p=@g -> return 7; same result without -bennett-closed-unit
```
**`driver-mixed-majors` (§19.8).** Produce the first module with LLVM 18 and the second with LLVM 23.
Both have the same datalayout and triple; M=23 reads and links both.
The linked result is 3+4=7.
Producing either module above envelope M, or changing its triple/datalayout to conflict, instead gives BD-E-VERSION.
Parsing these modules separately is not evidence of the mixed-major link.

```llvm example=driver-mixed-majors verdict=accept
target datalayout = "e-p:64:64"
target triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
define i32 @from18() {
  ret i32 3
}
```

```llvm example=driver-mixed-majors-second verdict=accept
target datalayout = "e-p:64:64"
target triple = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
declare i32 @from18()
define i32 @main() {
  %a = call i32 @from18()
  %r = add i32 %a, 4
  ret i32 %r
}
```

```text state=driver-mixed-majors at=0
driver: input from18.bc major=18; input from23.bc major=23; envelope newest M=23
read/link/plugin/runtime/arith major=23; common datalayout=e-p:64:64 triple=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
linked main -> return 7
conflicting triple or datalayout -> reject:BD-E-VERSION
input newer than M -> reject:BD-E-VERSION
```
**`platform-uart-write` (§20).** At the profile UART transmit window 0x10000000, N35 routes the volatile byte store to the model before N9.
It appends x (hex 78) to the console tape without a raw unallocated store.
With sufficient budgets and no pending interrupt, reverse restores the entry device/CSR state and empty tape.
This is a successful platform path; no typed R fault is assumed available in ISA 0.8.

```llvm example=platform-uart-write verdict=blocked:BD-B-ISA7 rmode=@main
define i32 @main() {
  %p = inttoptr i64 268435456 to ptr
  store volatile i8 120, ptr %p, align 1
  ret i32 0
}
```

```text blocker=platform-uart-write
BD-B-ISA7 R entry: BLK-5 (ISA-7); mandatory pre-instruction typed fault 1 requires ISA 0.9 K5 fault C, exact terminal code, no subsequent effects, preserved reversible prefix
```

```text state=platform-uart-write at=0
driver: --bennett-platform=riscv64-bennett-virt --bennett-tier=reversible --bennett-entry=main
entry: console=empty tape=empty; interrupts pending=none
materialisation: entry poll; volatile store -> MMIO helper -> UART model -> console.write
run: status=COMPLETED result=0 console=78; tape has console.write(78); no code 7
reverse: status=REVERSED console=empty tape=empty CSR=entry RAM=entry
```

`corpus/legality/` holds the cases (`cases/`: the 56 spike cases plus the `spec-*` cases of this document), four negative controls (`controls/`), the harness (`harness/run.py`), the trace runtime (`runtime/`) and the spike's results.

Spike cases use the provisional ABI v0 and arbitrary operation codes: they are **legality** cases (what LLVM passes do to marker programs), not well-formedness cases; the legality property (§3.6) does not depend on a marker's signature.
The harness selects the historical ABI v0 or ABI 0.2 trace runtime from each module's marker signatures; `spec-sem2-*` uses the budget-record ABI of §3.2 and the normative header.
The harness checks and their 0.2 reading:

L1 | the dynamic marker sequence and the classical result are preserved | unchanged; for cases whose marker operands are computed from floating point or query intrinsics, the baseline is the materialised module (§17.7)
L2 | no pass adds a forbidden attribute | the three lists of §3.6
L3 | handles stay contained (guard page, `BADHANDLE`; static review of new casts) | dynamic part unchanged; the static review is decided by §6
L4 | region identity | every region operand resolves (§7.2) to candidates content-equal (§7.3) to the baseline's: aliases, forwarding thunks and merged twins pass (harness relaxation, bd `-cjb`)
L5 | native code generation keeps L1 and every marker an undefined external | unchanged
L6 | region-operand shapes | every shape resolves (§7.2: the candidate set is bounded by the program)

**Supported envelope**: LLVM 18, 20 and 23; `default<O0>` … `default<O3>`; `default<Os>`, `default<Oz>` on 18 and 20 (LLVM 23's `opt` rejects them); `lto-pre-link<O3>`, `lto<O3>`, `thinlto-pre-link<O3>`, `thinlto<O3>`, `default<O3>` three times; clang `-O0` … `-O3` with `-flto`; rustc `-C opt-level` 0, 1, 2, 3, s, z, including its MergeFunctions in aliases mode; Julia 1.13's own pipeline; `strip`, `strip-nondebug` and `mergefunc` alone.

**Unsupported** (LLVM bugs outside the contract on every supported major; spike findings §2): the Attributor, module and CGSCC (llvm-project #234748, #236104, and on 18 and 20 the constant-table fold fixed by PR #151359); `normalize` without `preserve-order` (#236128); `structurizecfg` without its prerequisites; the passes the harness classes `non-preserving` and the sanitizer and instrumentation passes; any other single pass not run inside an envelope pipeline (§24 D20).

The **full version string** of this document (`0.2.10`) is the unit of compatibility: a plugin implements exactly one dialect version and targets exactly one ISA version (§19.9); drafts are not compatible with each other.
The S2 bitcast/initial-image repairs revise the full dialect to `0.2.10`.

The lifting map remains `0.2.9` (global-numbering correction); `norm`, `handles` and `regions` remain `0.2.8`; unchanged oracle-abi, tdl and effects remain `0.2.4`, marker/header, asm and corpus remain `0.2`, platform and driver remain `0.2.1`.
Every reference object is checked again; unchanged ISA-0.8 interface signatures retain their hashes.
The map version is recorded in certificate metadata, not inserted into ISA-owned interface signatures.

Every semantic change bumps the version; the reference objects and hashes of §16 depend on the ISA version string, the map and the layout, and change with any of them (0.1's hashes changed with the wrapper form of §16.2).

The build record (§19.9) records the runtimes, arith and asm-table hashes and the budget-table hash; `SPEC_VERSIONS.toml` records `dialect` and the targeted `isa`; the change rules are in `spec/README.md`.
Only mechanics appear here.
Each row states the capability it keeps; none has a default of reject, refuse, fault or no effect for something the north star promises.
